_Why can the network connecting accelerators matter more than the accelerators themselves at scale?_

A single accelerator can perform trillions of operations per second, but distributed training requires devices to exchange results before dependent work can proceed. When network capacity cannot keep pace with computation, accelerators sit idle, and adding more devices can increase the waiting instead of shortening the run. The resulting cost extends beyond the network equipment: an inexpensive connection can leave expensive compute capacity unused throughout a long experiment. Single-node intuition is insufficient because data that once traveled through a local interconnect must now cross cables, switches, and shared paths. A fast connection between two machines does not establish that the same performance will hold when the entire fleet communicates at once. The arrangement of those paths determines which groups can exchange data together and where competing transfers accumulate. Large transfers need sustained bandwidth, while frequent dependent exchanges can remain limited by the time required to start and complete each message. A delayed participant can hold up others even when most links appear healthy. Network design therefore has to follow the workload's communication pattern, and validation must reflect the traffic that will actually run. Choices about placement, sharing, and failure recovery affect whether available bandwidth becomes useful progress or recurring delay. In C³ terms, the fabric connects compute through communication, while coordination determines when the fleet must wait for that communication to finish.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}

## The Synchronization Backbone {#sec-network-fabrics-introduction}

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *

from mlsysim.fmt import MarkdownStr, check, fmt, fmt_int, fmt_math, fmt_memory, fmt_params

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
class NetworkRunningExampleCluster:
    """Archetype A reference (`Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference`): GPT-3 on Training_1K."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    _scn = Scenarios.DenseLLMPretrainingReference
    n_gpus = _scn.system.total_accelerators
    params = _scn.workload.parameters
    grad_bytes = _scn.workload.size_in_bytes(BYTES_FP16)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # The static TikZ/SVG figures in the transport section label 350 GB / 700 GB.
    check(abs(grad_bytes.to(GB).magnitude - 350) < 1e-6, "Static figures assume a 350 GB FP16 gradient")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    params_str = fmt_params(params)
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(n_gpus, commas=True, label="GPU")
    n_gpus_value_str = fmt(n_gpus, precision=0, commas=True)
    peer_gpus_str = fmt(n_gpus - 1, precision=0, commas=False)
    grad_gb_str = fmt_memory(grad_bytes, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/network_fabrics_gpu_fanout.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A schematic fan: one red source node on the left connects by six gray arrows to six blue nodes on the right, showing one node reaching many peers."}

*One slow link stalls every peer that waits on it.*
:::

@Sec-compute-infrastructure traced the bandwidth hierarchy down to the node boundary, where each GPU's NVLink bandwidth narrows to a single external network port. How much that narrowing costs depends on what the training job must push through the port, and how often. Consider the running instance of Archetype A (GPT-4/Llama-3), a `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.params_str`-parameter GPT-3-class dense transformer partitioned across the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_str` of the reference cluster. Each training step must combine gradient contributions so that corresponding model replicas apply the same update. This operation, called AllReduce, returns the combined result to every participating worker. The model has `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` of gradient data at two bytes per parameter, the 16-bit gradients of mixed-precision training that this chapter assumes throughout (FP32 gradients would double the figure). That model-wide figure is not what any one GPU sends. When a reduction partitions the gradient across all `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_value_str` ranks, each rank owns a 1/`{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_value_str` share, a few hundred megabytes, which is the gradient-shard size the transport examples below use; the job's tensor, pipeline, and data-parallel split (@sec-distributed-training-systems) sets each GPU's actual payload. Worked examples that switch to another model, precision, or payload state their parameters explicitly. A delayed transfer on the step's critical path can leave the other `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.peer_gpus_str` GPUs waiting at a job-wide synchronization boundary. The fabric's contribution to training time therefore depends on which transfers the next computation needs and how much of their cost remains exposed. In that role the fabric is not auxiliary infrastructure; it is the synchronization backbone that decides whether the cluster trains as one machine.

Within the multi-tier fleet hierarchy framed by @fig-fleet-stack, the fabric turns isolated accelerator nodes into a coherent training system. Accelerators, power delivery, cooling, racks, and pods define what each node can compute in isolation; the fabric determines whether the nodes can act together before communication cost overwhelms computation. That design space organizes into a **five-level model**\index{Five-level model!definition} of co-dependent tiers, developed in @sec-network-fabrics-five-level-model.

At scale, communication cost can dominate computation cost. The fleet-law decomposition in @sec-vol2-introduction-fleet-law makes this explicit: the nonoverlapped communication term $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount) - \OverlappedTime$ determines how much of each training step is exposed to the network fabric. The fabric influences the layers above it by determining whether communication can run while independent computation continues, which collective algorithms are viable, and how network partitions interact with node failures. That concurrency, communication-computation overlap\index{Communication-computation overlap!fabric role}, is what the $\OverlappedTime$ term credits, because transfer time that proceeds behind useful arithmetic does not lengthen the step.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ How layer-by-layer scheduling achieves that overlap, and how much communication it still leaves exposed, is developed in @sec-communication-overlap.
:::

A collective is a communication operation performed by a group of workers. Its name specifies the result each worker receives, while an algorithm determines the messages that produce that result. The physical network fabric carries three recurring collective communication patterns:

- **AllReduce**\index{AllReduce!fabric traffic pattern}: Combines corresponding values from all participants and returns the same result to each; synchronous training uses a sum, followed by normalization, to average gradient contributions across workers.
- **AllGather**\index{AllGather!fabric traffic pattern}: Collects a distinct portion from each participant and returns the concatenated collection to every participant, as required when reconstructing a sharded parameter tensor.
- **AllToAll**\index{AllToAll!fabric traffic pattern}: Lets each participant send a distinct portion to every other participant, an exchange central to expert parallelism when workers host different expert subnetworks and must route tokens to their assigned destinations.

Collective communication algorithms orchestrate these patterns, while the fabric layer supplies the physical wires and switches that carry them. The distinction matters because the fabric's physical properties (bandwidth, latency, and topology) determine which patterns are efficient and which become bottlenecks.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The full set of collective primitives, with the output contract each one guarantees, is developed in @sec-collective-communication-six-core-primitives-8a66.
:::

::: {#psp-network-fabrics-network-as-gradient-bus .callout-perspective title="The network as a gradient bus"}

In a single machine, the memory bus moves data between the processor and memory. In a distributed training cluster, the network fabric serves an analogous role as the gradient bus\index{Gradient!bus} that carries contributions between workers. When those exchanges limit progress, the job encounters the network wall\index{Communication wall!gradient bus} mapped across the pod tier in @fig-three-walls-grid. Protocols, topologies, congestion control, and collective schedules determine how effectively the job uses the available paths. This bus has a narrow segment. Since NVLink appeared, the external ports that join machines have offered less bandwidth than the interconnect inside each machine in every generation (@fig-network-bandwidth-scaling). How much of that gap a job actually feels depends on its message sizes, port provisioning, routing, and contention, so the link ratio bounds the problem rather than predicting a transfer time.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Communication dominance at scale, the network wall, is established in @sec-introduction-communication-becomes-dominant-e1b6.
:::

::: {#fig-network-bandwidth-scaling fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Historical Network Bandwidth Scaling**: Intra-node NVLink, inter-node InfiniBand and Ethernet, and the PCIe host bus, plotted per direction on a common log scale by the year each generation first shipped, 2010 to 2025. The aggregate NVLink budget exceeds the external-port budgets in these configurations; collective completion time also depends on payloads, provisioning, routing, and overlap. Rates and first-product years from IEEE 802.3, InfiniBand Trade Association, PCI-SIG, and NVIDIA specifications and product announcements." fig-alt="Log-scale chart of per-direction interconnect bandwidth from 2010 to 2025 for Ethernet, InfiniBand, NVLink, and PCIe, by first product year. ```{python}
#| echo: false
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
from mlsysim import viz

# Documented TIME slate (figure-visual-language §2.1); shared with @fig-alpha-beta-crossover.
SLATE_TIME = "#5E6B73"  # time/latency slate, same value as the margin-device TIME constant

from mlsysim import Literature

# Per-direction rates by first commercial product year: per port for Ethernet
# and InfiniBand, per x16 link after encoding for PCIe, and a GPU's summed
# links for NVLink. Within a family, the fastest generation shipping each year.
def _bandwidth_trend(rows):
    best = {}
    for r in rows:
        if r["first_product_year"] is None:
            continue
        fam = "PCIe (x16)" if r["family"] == "PCIe" else r["family"]
        key = (fam, int(r["first_product_year"]))
        best[key] = max(best.get(key, 0.0), r["line_rate_gbps"])
    out = [{"Year": y, "Technology": f, "Bandwidth_Gbps": v} for (f, y), v in best.items()]
    order = {"Ethernet": 0, "InfiniBand": 1, "NVLink": 2, "PCIe (x16)": 3}
    return pd.DataFrame(out).sort_values(["Technology", "Year"], key=lambda c: c.map(order) if c.name == "Technology" else c)

data = _bandwidth_trend(Literature.Series.InterconnectGenerations.entries)

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))
_groups = list(dict.fromkeys(data["Technology"]))
# Network links use the book's network hue (violet): NVLink solid, InfiniBand dashed with hollow markers;
# Ethernet in neutral slate and the PCIe host bus in dotted gray. Each series is
# labeled at its last point instead of in a legend.
_colors = {"NVLink": COLORS["VioletLine"], "InfiniBand": COLORS["VioletLine"], "Ethernet": SLATE_TIME, "PCIe (x16)": COLORS["secondary"]}
_styles = {"InfiniBand": "--", "PCIe (x16)": ":"}
_markers = {"PCIe (x16)": "s", "Ethernet": "D"}
_hollow = {"InfiniBand"}
# Series labels: NVLink and InfiniBand at their last point; Ethernet and PCIe
# (which end near InfiniBand) beside their early segments, in open space.
_label_at = {"Ethernet": (2013.2, 42, "center"), "PCIe (x16)": (2012.6, 228, "center")}
for _i, _g in enumerate(_groups):
    _sub = data[data["Technology"] == _g]
    _c = _colors.get(_g, COLORS["primary"])
    ax.plot(
        _sub["Year"],
        _sub["Bandwidth_Gbps"],
        color=_c,
        linestyle=_styles.get(_g, "-"),
        label=str(_g),
        marker=_markers.get(_g, "o"),
        markersize=5,
        markerfacecolor="white" if _g in _hollow else _c,
        markeredgewidth=1.4,
        linewidth=1.8,
    )
    if _g != "NVLink":
        continue  # the three external links run close together; they go in the legend
    else:
        ax.annotate(
            str(_g),
            (_sub["Year"].iloc[-1], _sub["Bandwidth_Gbps"].iloc[-1]),
            xytext=(7, 0),
            textcoords="offset points",
            va="center",
            ha="left",
            fontsize=9,
            color=_c,
            fontweight="bold",
        )
# The narrow segment of the gradient bus: shade the gap between NVLink and the
# InfiniBand port from NVLink's first year onward (log-space interpolation of
# the plotted points only; no new data), and mark where NVLink appears.
import numpy as np

_nv = data[data["Technology"] == "NVLink"]
_ib = data[data["Technology"] == "InfiniBand"]
_yrs = np.linspace(_nv["Year"].min(), _ib["Year"].max(), 200)
_nv_y = 10 ** np.interp(_yrs, _nv["Year"], np.log10(_nv["Bandwidth_Gbps"]))
_ib_y = 10 ** np.interp(_yrs, _ib["Year"], np.log10(_ib["Bandwidth_Gbps"]))
ax.fill_between(_yrs, _ib_y, _nv_y, color=COLORS["VioletL"], alpha=0.55, lw=0, zorder=0)
ax.text(
    2022.4,
    1550,
    "intra-node vs.\nexternal-port gap",
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS["VioletLine"],
    fontstyle="italic",
    linespacing=1.15,
)
_h, _l = ax.get_legend_handles_labels()
ax.legend(
    [h for h, l in zip(_h, _l) if l != "NVLink"], [l for l in _l if l != "NVLink"], loc="lower right", fontsize=9, frameon=True, framealpha=0.95
)
# The band's left edge marks where NVLink appears; point at its first plotted year.
ax.annotate(
    "NVLink appears",
    (_nv["Year"].min(), _nv["Bandwidth_Gbps"].min()),
    xytext=(2012.6, 2600),
    ha="center",
    va="center",
    fontsize=9,
    color=COLORS["primary"],
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-|>", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.9, shrinkA=4, shrinkB=5, connectionstyle="arc3,rad=-0.2"),
)
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_ylim(30, 12000)
ax.set_xlim(2009.5, 2027.6)
ax.set_xticks(range(2010, 2025, 2))
ax.set_ylabel("Bandwidth per direction (Gb/s)")
ax.set_xlabel("Year")
ax.grid(True, which="major", ls="--", alpha=0.5)
ax.grid(False, which="minor")
ax.yaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.LogLocator(base=10, subs=(1.0,)))
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda y, _: f"{int(y):,}"))
for _s in ("top", "right"):
    ax.spines[_s].set_visible(False)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
plt.close()

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-bandwidth-hierarchy
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ BANDWIDTH HIERARCHY SPECS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-introduction—the bandwidth cliff paragraph,
# │          and pervasive IB NDR bandwidth references throughout the chapter.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute the bandwidth hierarchy (NVLink vs IB vs HBM) and the
# │       NVLink-to-IB ratio that defines the intra/inter-node cliff.
# │ Show: ~400 Gb/s NDR, ~50 GB/s NDR, ~900 GB/s NVLink, ~9x per-direction ratio.
# │ How: Preserve Pint quantities; extract only the dimensionless ratio.
# │
# │ Used by: @sec-network-fabrics-introduction (line ~173), and IB NDR
# │          bandwidth refs in Level 1, Level 2, Level 5, Virtualization,
# │          Monitoring, Fallacies sections.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_flop_rate

class NetworkFabricsContextScenario:
    """Bandwidth hierarchy specs for the chapter-wide fabric discussion."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_raw = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth  # 50 GB/s per port (per direction)
    nvlink_h100_raw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth  # 900 GB/s datasheet bidirectional total
    nvlink_h100_perdir = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth_per_direction  # 450 GB/s one-way
    h100_flops_raw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.compute.peak_flops
    h100_mem_bw_raw = Hardware.Cloud.H100.memory.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    # Honest cliff = like-with-like, both per-direction: NVLink 450 GB/s vs an
    # NDR port's 50 GB/s = 9x. (Comparing NVLink's 900 GB/s bidirectional total
    # against the per-direction port rate would double-count to a spurious 18x.)
    nvlink_to_ib_ratio_val = (nvlink_h100_perdir / ib_ndr_raw).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(ib_ndr_raw > 300 * Gbps, "NDR BW should exceed 300 Gb/s")
    check(nvlink_to_ib_ratio_val > 8, "Per-direction NVLink-to-IB cliff should be ~9x")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(ib_ndr_raw, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(ib_ndr_raw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_h100_raw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink_h100_perdir, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    nvlink_to_ib_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(nvlink_to_ib_ratio_val, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str = fmt_flop_rate(h100_flops_raw, unit=TFLOP / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    h100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(h100_mem_bw_raw, unit=TB / second, precision=2, commas=False)
```

The reference hardware gives the gradient bus analogy a concrete scale. A single H100 has a precision-specific FP16 peak of `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.h100_fp16_tflop_per_s_str` and memory bandwidth of `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.h100_mem_bw_tb_per_s_str`. Each GPU's NVLink ports together provide `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str` of bidirectional bandwidth to its peers within the node. The comparison that matters is per GPU and per direction. In the reference node each GPU has its own network interface card (NIC) with one NDR InfiniBand port, so a tensor leaving the node through that GPU drops from `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.nvlink_h100_perdir_gb_per_s_str` of NVLink bandwidth to `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` at the port. This `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.nvlink_to_ib_ratio_mult_str` gap is the node boundary's cliff that the bandwidth hierarchy of @sec-compute-bandwidth-hierarchy already identified. The model-wide `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient state does not all pass through every `{python} NetworkFabricsContextScenario.ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str` port; partitioning and the collective schedule determine each port's traffic. Converting that gap into a step-time estimate requires the workload's local payloads and communication dependencies.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The network hierarchy ratio between intra-node and inter-node bandwidth, with the reference NVLink and InfiniBand values behind it, is developed in @sec-appdx-fleet-foundations-numbers-to-know.
:::

Which traffic must cross that gap depends on how the job is partitioned. The same hierarchy keeps tensor parallelism, with its per-layer exchanges, inside the NVLink domain and lets pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas span nodes, the combination called 3D parallelism whose schedules are developed in @sec-distributed-training-systems-systems-hybrid-parallelism-3d-loop. The fabric adds one lever to that placement. Each data-parallel replica can sum gradients over several microbatches before an exchange (gradient accumulation\index{Gradient accumulation!communication frequency}), reducing how often it must cross the node boundary at the cost of changing the batch and update schedule.

Exposed communication leaves gaps between dependent compute phases. Two assumed training schedules on a common 230 ms axis, each containing 100 ms forward and backward compute phases, make that cost visible (@fig-bandwidth-cliff-gantt). The 8-GPU intra-node case assumes a 1 ms AllReduce and spends 99.5 percent of the step in those compute phases; the 64-GPU inter-node case assumes a 30 ms AllReduce and spends 87 percent in computation. The two AllReduce durations are illustrative inputs chosen to show the effect, not values derived from the link rates above, and the percentages are shares of the schedule rather than measured arithmetic utilization.

::: {#fig-bandwidth-cliff-gantt fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Bandwidth Cliff in a Training Step**: Illustrative timelines on a common millisecond axis for the same compute phases: an 8-GPU intra-node job (top) with an assumed 1 ms AllReduce, and a 64-GPU inter-node job (bottom) with an assumed 30 ms AllReduce. These durations illustrate an exposed communication cost rather than predict a particular fabric. The AllReduce phase (red) grows from a thin sliver to a larger share of the step. Without overlap, model computation waits during AllReduce. The compute phases occupy 99.5 percent and 87 percent of these illustrative schedules, a gap of 12.5 percentage points; these shares are not arithmetic utilization measurements." fig-alt="Two illustrative horizontal Gantt rows drawn to scale on a shared time axis marked 0, 100, 200, and 230, labeled Time (ms). The top row, labeled Intra-node, 8 GPUs, NVLink, and 99.5% compute, shows Forward (100 ms) and Backward (100 ms) blocks followed by a thin red AllReduce (1 ms) sliver. The bottom row, labeled Inter-node, 64 GPUs, IB, and 87% compute, shows the same Forward and Backward blocks followed by a wider red AllReduce (30 ms) block, with a red brace beneath it labeled 30 ms idle per step."}

![](images/svg/bandwidth-cliff-gantt.svg){width="100%"}

:::

In Fleet Law terms, the widened red block is the part of $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$ that no $\OverlappedTime$ has hidden. In the inter-node schedule it is 30 ms of every 230 ms step, about 13 percent, and that share applies to every accelerator-hour the cluster spends for the life of the run. Network fabric design therefore belongs at the center of distributed-training design rather than at its edge.

## How ML Networking Inverts Data-Center Assumptions {#sec-network-workload-inversion}

A network provisioned for many independent requests can encounter a different load when a training job releases gradient exchanges together. Statistical multiplexing relies on traffic peaks not all coinciding; synchronized workers can instead compete for the same paths at the same time. Web services also have dependency chains and tail-latency requirements, but a bulk-synchronous training job makes the participating workers' shared completion boundary explicit.

The ML networking inversion\index{ML networking!data-center workload inversion} in @tbl-network-assumptions concerns this change in traffic dependencies. Synchronous collective phases can generate correlated bursts and long-lived flows whose completion gates the next computation. Fabric validation must therefore measure collective completion under the expected load; average per-flow throughput alone does not establish that the job can meet its step-time budget.

| **Workload pattern**   | **Traditional data-center assumption**                 | **ML reality**                                                    |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Traffic pattern**    | Independent requests can arrive asynchronously         | Collective phases can release correlated bursts                   |
| **Flow type**          | Many short transfers can share available paths         | Large collective transfers can create persistent "elephant" flows |
| **Performance metric** | Per-request completion and throughput                  | Collective completion and exposed step time                       |
| **Loss tolerance**     | Recovery delays affected requests                      | Recovery can delay dependent workers at a barrier                 |
| **Congestion**         | Statistical multiplexing relies on noncoincident peaks | Shared paths and fan-in can concentrate synchronized traffic      |

: **ML Networking Inverts Traditional Data-Center Assumptions**: The comparison contrasts independent-request traffic with synchronized collective phases. Correlated demand and shared completion boundaries change the fabric's capacity and latency requirements. {#tbl-network-assumptions}

The bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)[^fn-bsp-valiant-routing] model, the lockstep at step barriers already met at the scale of one node (@sec-compute-node), makes the dependency in @tbl-network-assumptions explicit. In the synchronous training example, all `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_str` must complete the required gradient exchange before the next step can proceed. A 100 ms transfer delay adds 100 ms to that step only if it extends the critical path by the full interval; other computation or communication may hide part of it. At a barrier that waits for the last required result, **tail latency**\index{Tail latency!definition}\index{P99!definition}, the slow end of the completion-time distribution (commonly reported as its 99th percentile, p99), decides when the step ends, so at such a barrier the tail cannot be dismissed as an outlier.

[^fn-bsp-valiant-routing]: [offset=-14mm] **BSP (bulk synchronous parallel)**\index{Bulk synchronous parallel!origin}: Proposed by @valiant1990 as a bridging model between parallel hardware and software. Synchronous data-parallel training follows the same barrier structure [@goyal2017accurate; @li2020pytorch].
