:::

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-bulk-synchronous-parallel-bsp .callout-definition title="Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)"}

***Bulk synchronous parallel (BSP)***\index{Bulk synchronous parallel!definition} is a parallel execution model in which every worker completes a local computation phase, exchanges the data required by the next phase, and then waits at a global barrier before any worker begins the next phase, which makes the slowest participant the pacing constraint for the entire cluster.

1.  **Significance**: The slowest required computation or communication determines when a superstep can complete. Faster workers wait at the barrier, so a localized delay can consume idle accelerator time across the entire participating group.
2.  **Distinction**: BSP organizes execution into synchronized supersteps; it does not itself prescribe a learning algorithm or a particular exchange pattern. Synchronous data-parallel updates match a single-device reference only under compatible global batches, update rules, and numerical assumptions.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Removing barriers does not by itself establish faster time-to-quality. Asynchronous training trades waiting against stale updates, and the convergence and wall-clock comparison depends on the workload and update schedule.

:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↩ Synchronous tight coupling, the shared step barrier that lets the slowest worker pace a training fleet, is established in @sec-introduction-traditional-vs-ml-fleet-dynamics-c43e.
:::

The flow inversion compounds this problem. Traditional networks are designed for fairness among millions of "mice flows,"\index{Mice flow!network traffic}[^fn-elephant-flow-collision] yet ML training is dominated by a few "elephant flows"\index{Elephant flow!gradient AllReduce} corresponding to the gradient AllReduce. The full 175B model has `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` of gradient state at the assumed precision, but a sharded job distributes that state across workers. Each collective operates on its participating group and local payload; its algorithm determines how much each worker sends. Standard flow control and routing mechanisms like equal-cost multi-path (ECMP)\index{ECMP!elephant flow limitations}\index{Multi-path routing|see{ECMP}}\index{Equal-cost multi-path|see{ECMP}}, which hash each flow onto one of several equal-cost paths, are poorly suited to this traffic pattern. A static hash\index{ECMP!hash polarization} cannot subdivide one elephant flow across all available links, and it can inadvertently map multiple elephant flows to the same link, creating massive congestion while other links sit idle.

[^fn-elephant-flow-collision]: [offset=2mm] **Elephant and mice flows**\index{Elephant and mice flows!definition}: The model-wide gradient size is not the size of one network flow. A collective can split each worker's local gradient shard across channels and transport connections; the resulting long-lived flows\index{Elephant flow!network traffic} can still collide under ECMP when their static hashes select the same path.

The loss inversion completes the picture. TCP was designed to recover across an unreliable network, and an occasional retransmission delays only the request it belongs to. In a synchronous collective, a lost packet delays the transfer that every waiting worker needs, and some NICs that implement remote direct memory access (RDMA), called RDMA NICs or RNICs, recover by resending everything after the missing packet rather than only the lost region (Go-Back-N-style recovery). ML fabrics therefore aim to make loss rare and recovery bounded, either by preventing buffer overflow at the link layer or by building transports that recover quickly from it. Level 2 (@sec-network-fabrics-losslessness) develops both approaches.

::: {.content-visible when-format="pdf"}
\newpage
:::

Correlated demand also makes **oversubscription**\index{Oversubscription!definition}, provisioning less uplink capacity at a switch tier than the downlink capacity it serves (written as a downlink:uplink ratio such as 2:1), a workload decision. A fabric with spare capacity under independent requests can become saturated when a collective releases traffic across the same cut. Designing for that traffic requires tracing the constraint from the wire through transport, topology, and congestion control to the job's synchronization boundary.

### The five-level model {#sec-network-fabrics-five-level-model}

Provisioning fast NICs or buying a non-blocking switch tier in isolation routinely fails to speed up training: a 400 Gb/s link still stalls if host TCP copies starve the PCIe bus, an unaligned rack layout exhausts the copper link budget, or static ECMP hashing piles two elephant flows onto one spine port. Tracing why a collective slows down requires following the packet across five coupled layers, from serializer/deserializer (SerDes) signaling and copper or optical reach at Level 1 to the integration of a production cluster at Level 5 (@fig-network-five-level-model). Each level is developed at the point where its physical or protocol limit becomes the binding constraint.

::: {#fig-network-five-level-model fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The Five-Level Network Model for ML Training**: Read from the bottom up, each level builds on the one below and becomes more abstract. Level 1 moves bits over wires and optics; Level 2 turns links into reliable, low-overhead transfers between accelerators; Level 3 arranges switches into a topology; Level 4 governs how the fabric behaves under load and congestion; and Level 5 integrates all of them into a production cluster." fig-alt="Five stacked horizontal bands, labeled L1 at the bottom to L5 at the top, with an upward arrow labeled more abstract. L1, wire and link: PAM4 SerDes, copper DAC, AOC, optics. L2, transport: RDMA, RoCEv2, GPUDirect, alpha-beta cost model. L3, switch and topology: fat-tree, rail-optimized, dragonfly, torus. L4, fabric behavior: PFC, ECN and DCQCN, incast, adaptive routing. L5, cluster design: pod integration, job placement, failure domains. Beside each band a small schematic shows the level's concrete form: L1, a four-level stepped waveform between two transceivers labeled SerDes; L2, a GPU and its NIC, both labeled, sending to a remote NIC and GPU; L3, two switches linked to all four switches below them; L4, three converging inputs feeding a nearly full queue, with a dashed red arrow labeled PAUSE leaving the queue and pointing back over the inputs; L5, a row of six racks joined by a common bar."}
![](images/svg/five-level-model.svg)

:::

Each inversion of @tbl-network-assumptions traces back to a specific physical or protocol constraint, and the five levels locate where each one is paid:

- **Level 1: wire and link** (@sec-network-fabrics-wire-link). Signal integrity (PAM4, SerDes), forward error correction, and the reach of copper and optics impose hard constraints on per-hop latency and cluster geometry.
- **Level 2: transport** (@sec-network-fabrics-transport). InfiniBand and RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) provide RDMA primitives; the $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ model quantifies the latency-vs.-bandwidth trade-off for different message sizes.
- **Level 3: switch and topology** (@sec-network-fabrics-topology). Fat-trees, rail-optimized designs, and dragonflies achieve the $\BisectionBandwidth$ needed for global collectives through different structural trade-offs.
- **Level 4: fabric behavior** (@sec-network-fabrics-behavior). Link-level flow control and end-to-end congestion control determine whether theoretical bandwidth translates to realized throughput; adaptive routing and incast behavior determine whether that throughput survives real collective traffic [@alizadeh2010; @zhu2015; @li2019; @gangidi2024rdma].
- **Level 5: cluster design** (@sec-network-fabrics-cluster). Production supercomputers like the NVIDIA SuperPOD and Meta Grand Teton integrate these layers into a unified gradient bus [@nvidia2023dgxSuperpodH100; @meta2024genaiInfrastructure].

The levels are not an inventory of networking topics; they are the causal chain that turns synchronous ML traffic into infrastructure requirements. Large gradient messages first stress the wire and transport, then force topology choices that preserve bisection bandwidth, then expose congestion behavior that ordinary enterprise networks can hide, and finally determine whether the whole cluster behaves like one training machine.

The traffic pattern determines which fabric metric matters. A global reduction stresses bisection bandwidth and the slowest path; a point-to-point pipeline transfer sits on the critical path, so its full transfer time and hop count matter; an expert exchange stresses path diversity and egress balance; and checkpoint or tenant traffic stresses isolation from the synchronization path (@tbl-network-fabrics-traffic-metrics). The remaining levels develop each of these pairings in turn.

| **Traffic pattern**                 | **Fabric pressure**                    | **Metric that predicts performance**                        | **Primary design response**                                       |
|:------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------|
| Global reduction                    | Sustained traffic across a cluster cut | delivered bisection bandwidth; slowest-path completion time | non-blocking capacity, rail alignment, topology-aware collectives |
| Pipeline point-to-point             | Critical-path activation handoffs      | startup latency plus size/bandwidth; hop count              | short paths, direct placement, transport offload                  |
| Expert AllToAll                     | Many simultaneous worker pairs         | path utilization; egress queue depth; tail latency          | adaptive routing, path diversity, balanced expert placement       |
| Checkpoint and multi-tenant traffic | Bursts competing with training flows   | per-class bandwidth; pause duration; interference           | traffic classes (virtual lanes, QoS), admission control           |

: **Traffic Patterns Determine Fabric Metrics**: Workload semantics translate into different physical bottlenecks, so no single link-rate benchmark predicts training performance. The table is a map of what follows; the mechanisms in its right two columns (transport offload, adaptive routing, virtual lanes, and the rest) are developed at Levels 2 through 5. {#tbl-network-fabrics-traffic-metrics tbl-colwidths="[20,27,28,25]"}

Mapping workload semantics to physical constraints shows why ML fabric design must proceed from the physical layer up. Before higher-level topologies or routing protocols can organize traffic, the physical layer must reliably deliver bits between endpoints without excessive signal attenuation or prohibitive power consumption. Level 1 begins where all fabric architecture originates: at the physical wire.

## Level 1 Wire and Link {#sec-network-fabrics-wire-link}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Wire/link section — 175B cluster GPU count
class NetworkWireClusterRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators, commas=True, label="GPU")
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Wire and link — NDR line rate references.
class IbNdrWireRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

At `{python} IbNdrWireRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` and beyond, the physics of signal transmission imposes hard limits on cable length, power consumption, and error rates. Signal attenuation in copper and chromatic dispersion in fiber dictate how far an accelerator can sit from its switches before communication fails. Every higher-level protocol and topology is ultimately constrained by what the physical wire can carry; these limits shape the geometry of the entire cluster. To meet throughput demands without raising the signaling rate into worse attenuation, link designs must carry more bits in each transmitted symbol.

### Signal integrity and PAM4 {#sec-network-fabrics-pam4}

Achieving `{python} IbNdrWireRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` and higher line rates requires balancing signaling speed against channel loss and detection errors. The **symbol rate**\index{Symbol rate!definition} counts transmitted symbols per second; consecutive symbols need not produce a voltage transition. Raising the symbol rate raises the frequencies the channel must carry, and copper loses more signal at higher frequencies. Carrying more bits in each symbol, by using more than two signal levels, raises the bit rate without that penalty, and PAM4\index{PAM4 signaling!symbol rate} is the scheme high-speed links use to do it.

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-pam4-signaling .callout-definition title="PAM4 signaling"}

***PAM4 signaling***\index{PAM4 signaling!definition}\index{PAM4|see{PAM4 signaling}}\index{PAM4 modulation|see{PAM4 signaling}} is a modulation scheme that represents two bits per symbol with four signal levels, doubling the raw bit rate relative to binary signaling at the same symbol rate.

1.  **Significance**: PAM4 increases the raw $\Bandwidth$ available at a given symbol rate. The reduced separation between levels makes error-control design part of that gain. High-speed Ethernet uses forward error correction (FEC)\index{Forward error correction!Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)}, including Reed-Solomon RS(544,514), with processing latency that depends on the physical-layer (PHY) design and implementation [@anslow2016rsFec; @yin2022fecRequirements]. FEC contributes to the fixed path budget modeled by the $\MessageStartupLatency$ term in @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model; it is one component alongside propagation, switching, and endpoint processing.
2.  **Distinction**: At equal symbol rate and voltage swing, NRZ (Non-Return-to-Zero) binary signaling carries one bit per symbol with greater separation between levels. PAM4\index{PAM4 signaling!noise margin trade-off} carries two bits per symbol with smaller level spacing; the link must compensate through its signal-quality and error-correction design.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Doubling bits per symbol does not guarantee twice the usable payload throughput or a fixed latency penalty. Coding overhead, channel quality, and the chosen PHY implementation determine delivered performance.

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_time

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: PAM4 / FEC latency paragraph.
class FECLatency:
    FEC_LATENCY_LOW = Systems.SwitchFabric.FecLatencyLow
    FEC_LATENCY_HIGH = Systems.SwitchFabric.FecLatencyHigh
    ns_low = FEC_LATENCY_LOW
    ns_high = FEC_LATENCY_HIGH
    three_hops = 3
    round_trip_hops = 6
    three_hop_low = ns_low * three_hops
    three_hop_high = ns_high * three_hops
    round_trip_low = ns_low * round_trip_hops
    round_trip_high = ns_high * round_trip_hops
    check(round(three_hop_low.to(nanosecond).magnitude) == 300, "Three-hop one-way FEC lower bound should be 300 ns")
    check(round(round_trip_high.to(nanosecond).magnitude) == 1200, "Six-hop round-trip FEC upper bound should be 1200 ns")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    three_hop_low_ns_str = fmt_time(three_hop_low, nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    three_hop_high_ns_str = fmt_time(three_hop_high, nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    round_trip_low_ns_str = fmt_time(round_trip_low, nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    round_trip_high_ns_str = fmt_time(round_trip_high, nanosecond, precision=0, commas=False)
```

The price is noise margin. With four levels packed into the same voltage swing, the gap between adjacent levels in PAM4\index{PAM4 signaling!voltage levels} shrinks to one third of the NRZ gap (@fig-pam4-vs-nrz), making the link highly susceptible to noise. Consequently, high-speed links operate near the physical limits of reliable detection and require **forward error correction (FEC)**\index{Forward error correction!definition}\index{FEC!definition} at the physical layer, commonly using Reed-Solomon RS(544,514)-family codes in high-speed Ethernet designs [@anslow2016rsFec; @ethernetAlliance2025roadmap]. FEC processing is an implementation-dependent latency term; IEEE 802.3df operator material treats roughly 100 ns of host-side FEC with the RS(544,514) code (called KP4 in the standard) and hundreds of nanoseconds of end-to-end module latency as meaningful at AI/HPC fabric timescales [@yin2022fecRequirements]. Because each switch on a path decodes and re-encodes the signal, the FEC cost accumulates with the number of switches a packet traverses. A path's length is its **hop count**\index{Hop count!definition}, counted as switch traversals or as inter-switch links; where the two counts differ, each example states which one it uses. A packet that traverses three switches, the leaf-spine-leaf route of a two-tier fabric, incurs a scenario budget of `{python} FECLatency.three_hop_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.three_hop_high_ns_str` of one-way FEC latency, or `{python} FECLatency.round_trip_low_ns_str`--`{python} FECLatency.round_trip_high_ns_str` for a round trip. Against the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient of the 175B job, a few hundred nanoseconds are negligible, because bulk transfers are governed by bandwidth. The cost lands instead on small, latency-bound messages, such as the control handoffs that coordinate pipeline stages, and on collectives whose many sequential steps each pay it. This physical-layer latency sets a floor on the fabric's fixed startup latency, formalized in @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model as the $\MessageStartupLatency$ term, that no software optimization can remove.

::: {#fig-pam4-vs-nrz fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**From NRZ to PAM4 Signaling**: Both panels send six symbols in the same time over the same total voltage swing. NRZ (left) uses two levels and carries one bit per symbol, 6 bits in all; PAM4 (right) uses four levels and carries two bits per symbol, 12 bits in all, doubling the data rate without raising the symbol rate. The cost is noise margin: adjacent PAM4 levels sit one third as far apart (arrows), so high-speed links need forward error correction (FEC), which adds to the fabric's fixed $\MessageStartupLatency$ latency." fig-alt="Two waveform panels with six equal symbol slots marked by dashed vertical lines. Left, NRZ: a square wave switching between levels 1 and 0, with one tall shaded band between the two levels and an arrow labeled full swing; below, a strip of six cells holds the bits 1, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1, labeled 6 bits. Right, PAM4: a stepped wave among four levels labeled 00, 01, 10, and 11, with three thin shaded bands between adjacent levels and an arrow labeled one-third swing across one band; below, a strip of twelve cells grouped in pairs holds two bits per symbol, labeled 12 bits."}
![](images/svg/pam4-vs-nrz.svg)

:::

Doubling line rate without doubling the symbol rate therefore trades signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for bandwidth, and forward error correction\index{Forward error correction!channel limit} is what lets the link operate that close to the channel limit. Because that tighter margin leaves less room for channel attenuation, it also shortens the distance a passive copper cable can span before the link must switch to optics.

### Reach and medium for copper and optics {#sec-network-fabrics-copper-optics}

\index{Direct attach copper|see{DAC}}\index{Active optical cable|see{AOC}}Past one to three meters, passive copper attenuates high-frequency PAM4 signals beyond what even FEC can recover, forcing any link that exits a rack onto active optical cables or pluggable optics at a steep jump in cost and power. The choice of physical medium therefore determines how far a link can reach before latency, power, and cabling budgets reshape the cluster geometry, and the recurring cable and optics options differ along exactly those attributes (@tbl-network-fabrics-link-media).

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-spine-optics-cost

# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SPINE-LAYER OPTICS COST AND POWER
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @psp-network-fabrics-cost-distance — the "cost of distance"
# │          perspective quantifying spine-layer optics for a 10K-GPU cluster.
# │
# │ Goal: Compute the spine-optics dollar and power totals from the registry
# │       pluggable-optics power (the old prose hand-typed 10 W/link — the
# │       CPO value — and derived 200 kW where the registry 20 W gives 400 kW,
# │       contradicting the OpticalDividend cell later in this chapter).
# │ Show: Link count, power per selected endpoint, cabling cost, endpoint power subtotal.
# │ How: Derive the spine link count from the 10K training cluster; per-link
# │      optics, DAC, and AOC prices come from Infrastructure.Pricing.Network;
# │      one selected spine-side module per link uses OpticsPluggable400G; rack power
# │      bounds come from Infrastructure.Racks.AI_Standard / AI_High.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_power, fmt_qty_range, fmt_usd

class SpineOpticsCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_10K.total_accelerators
    n_links = 2 * cluster_gpus  # scenario assumption: two spine-layer optical links per accelerator
    link_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Network.OpticsPerLinkUsd.rate  # per-link optics cost
    dac_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Network.DacCableUsd.rate  # passive copper cable
    aoc_cost = Infrastructure.Pricing.Network.AocCableUsd.rate  # active optical cable
    link_power = Systems.SwitchFabric.OpticsPluggable400G  # one selected spine-side module per link; opposite end excluded
    rack_power_low = Infrastructure.Racks.AI_Standard.power_kw * kW  # dense AI rack lower bound
    rack_power_high = Infrastructure.Racks.AI_High.power_kw * kW  # dense AI rack upper bound

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    total_cost = n_links * link_cost
    total_power = n_links * link_power

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(total_power.to(kW).magnitude == 400, "20,000 selected spine-side modules at registry power should draw 400 kW")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    cluster_gpus_str = fmt_count(cluster_gpus, label="GPU", commas=True)
    n_links_str = fmt(n_links, precision=0, commas=True)
    link_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(link_cost, precision=0, commas=False)
    dac_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(dac_cost, precision=0, commas=False)
    aoc_cost_usd_str = fmt_usd(aoc_cost, precision=0, commas=False)
    link_power_w_str = fmt_power(link_power, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
    total_cost_musd_str = fmt_usd(total_cost, precision=0, commas=False, scale="million")
    total_power_kw_str = fmt_power(total_power, unit=kW, precision=0, commas=False)
    rack_power_range_str = fmt_qty_range(rack_power_low, rack_power_high, kW, precision=0, commas=False)
```

| **Medium**                                              | **Reach**                                   | **Cost profile**                                                                                                                                                    | **Latency impact**                                                                      | **Typical placement**            |
|:--------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| **DAC (direct attach copper)**\index{DAC!definition}    | 1 to 3 meters, shrinking as lane rate rises | Lowest cost (~`{python} SpineOpticsCost.dac_cost_usd_str`) and no optical module power                                                                              | Lowest media latency; no optical conversion, though high-speed lanes still pay FEC      | Within a rack                    |
| **AOC (active optical cable)**\index{AOC!definition}    | 3 to 30 meters                              | Higher cost (~`{python} SpineOpticsCost.aoc_cost_usd_str`) from permanently attached transceivers (the modules that convert between electrical and optical signals) | Electrical/optical conversion adds latency on top of the forward error correction (FEC) | Rack-to-rack or row-scale links  |
| **Pluggable optics**\index{Pluggable optics!definition} | More than 30 meters                         | Highest module and power cost, but replaceable optics and fiber cords                                                                                               | Optical conversion adds latency on top of FEC; distance enables topology reach          | Network core and pod-scale links |

: **Cable and Optics Placement Trade-Offs**: Common interconnect media occupy different reach, latency, and cost points, so cluster designers use copper inside racks and optics as distance begins to dominate placement. {#tbl-network-fabrics-link-media tbl-colwidths="[18,20,20,20,22]"}

The high-speed copper and optical paths considered here both include FEC\index{FEC!optical latency budget}, so choosing optics does not by itself remove error-correction overhead. The ranges in @tbl-network-fabrics-link-media describe representative placements rather than fixed boundaries between media. Optical interconnects\index{Optical interconnect!reach and latency} can extend the layout beyond a passive copper channel's budget, while pluggable optics\index{Pluggable optics!reach and cost} also permit separate replacement of modules and fiber. Reach, delivered latency, power, and serviceability jointly determine the choice.

```{=latex}
\Needspace{30\baselineskip}
```

::: {#psp-network-fabrics-cost-distance .callout-perspective title="The cost of distance"}

In an ML fleet, distance is money. Assuming two spine-layer optical links per accelerator, a cluster of `{python} SpineOpticsCost.cluster_gpus_str` requires ~`{python} SpineOpticsCost.n_links_str` optical links at the spine layer alone. At `{python} SpineOpticsCost.link_cost_usd_str` per complete link, that represents `{python} SpineOpticsCost.total_cost_musd_str` in cabling. For power, count one selected spine-side pluggable module per link at `{python} SpineOpticsCost.link_power_w_str` per module\index{Pluggable optics!transceiver power}, giving `{python} SpineOpticsCost.total_power_kw_str` for those endpoints alone. Each optical link also has a module at its opposite end; this subtotal excludes those modules, switch electronics, and cooling, so it is not the full fabric power budget. The cost dictates cluster geometry\index{Cluster!geometry}: architects pack accelerators as densely as possible (`{python} SpineOpticsCost.rack_power_range_str` per rack) to maximize cheap copper and minimize expensive optics.

:::

### SerDes, link budget, and power {#sec-network-fabrics-serdes}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-serdes-power-budget
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SERDES POWER BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-serdes — the SerDes/interconnect power
# │          paragraph below.
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the interconnect power draw for the running-example cluster
# │       and express it as a fraction of the GPU power budget.
# │ Show: 350 GB AllReduce, ~3,000 links, one selected 25 W port/link, 75 kW subtotal,
# │       ~10 percent of the accelerator power budget.
# │ How: gradient = GPT3 params × 2 bytes (FP16); link count and per-port power
# │      are scenario assumptions; GPU power budget = total_accelerators × TDP.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_memory, fmt_percent, fmt_power

class SerDesPowerBudget:
    """Interconnect SerDes/transceiver power for the 175B running-example cluster."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    h100_tdp = Hardware.Cloud.H100.tdp
    gradient = Models.Language.GPT3.parameters * (2 * byte / param)  # 175B FP16 AllReduce
    n_links = 3000  # scenario assumption: high-speed links to sustain full BW_bisect
    port_power = 25 * watt  # scenario assumption: combined SerDes + optics at one selected switch-side port per link

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    interconnect_power = n_links * port_power
    gpu_power_budget = n_gpus * h100_tdp
    power_fraction = (interconnect_power / gpu_power_budget).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(gradient.to(GB).magnitude - 350) < 1e-6, "175B FP16 AllReduce should be 350 GB")
    check(interconnect_power.to(kW).magnitude == 75, "3,000 selected switch-side ports at 25 W should draw 75 kW")
    check(0.10 < power_fraction < 0.11, f"Interconnect should be ~10 percent of GPU power, got {power_fraction:.3f}")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    grad_gb_str = fmt_memory(gradient, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_links_str = fmt(n_links, precision=0, commas=True)
    port_power_w_str = fmt_power(port_power, unit=watt, precision=0, commas=False)
    interconnect_kw_str = fmt_power(interconnect_power, unit=kW, precision=0, commas=False)
    power_frac_pct_str = fmt_percent(power_fraction, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
```

Driving thousands of high-speed links across a cluster burns tens of kilowatts just to serialize bits onto the wire, rivaling a noticeable share of the accelerators' own thermal budget. Every port depends on a **serializer/deserializer (SerDes)**\index{SerDes!definition}\index{Serializer/Deserializer|see{SerDes}} circuit that converts parallel data from the switch application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) into a serial stream, and its power cost accumulates across the provisioned ports. For the `{python} NetworkWireClusterRecap.n_gpus_str` reference cluster, assume a full-$\BisectionBandwidth$ fabric with roughly `{python} SerDesPowerBudget.n_links_str` high-speed links across its host and switch tiers. Count one selected switch-side port per link in this power subtotal. Each counted `{python} IbNdrWireRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` port is assigned `{python} SerDesPowerBudget.port_power_w_str`, more than the `{python} SpineOpticsCost.link_power_w_str` pluggable-module figure in the cost-of-distance estimate because it also counts the switch-side SerDes that drives the module. The model totals `{python} SerDesPowerBudget.interconnect_kw_str`, equivalent to `{python} SerDesPowerBudget.power_frac_pct_str` of the accelerators' combined thermal design power. This comparison isolates the assumed power of the selected switch-side ports, excluding the opposite endpoints and the rest of the switch chassis; it does not establish total fabric power or the fraction of measured cluster energy consumed by networking.

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Link-budget paragraph below — dB allowance for one copper lane.
class LinkBudgetScenario:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    budget_db = 30  # scenario assumption: end-to-end loss allowance for one 50G PAM4 lane
    cable_m = 3  # scenario assumption: passive DAC length
    cable_loss_db = 18  # scenario assumption: insertion loss of that cable at the lane's Nyquist frequency
    connector_loss_db = 2  # scenario assumption: combined connector loss
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    margin_db = budget_db - cable_loss_db - connector_loss_db
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(margin_db > 0, "Scenario link must close with positive margin")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    budget_db_str = MarkdownStr(f"{budget_db} dB")
    cable_m_str = MarkdownStr(f"{cable_m}-meter")
    cable_loss_db_str = MarkdownStr(f"{cable_loss_db} dB")
    connector_loss_db_str = MarkdownStr(f"{connector_loss_db} dB")
    margin_db_str = MarkdownStr(f"{margin_db} dB")
```

The **link budget**\index{Link budget!definition} allocates the signal loss a path can tolerate while meeting its error target. Losses are counted in decibels (dB), a logarithmic power ratio in which every 10 dB is a further tenfold attenuation (3 dB is roughly a halving), so the losses of cables and connectors in series add directly. In this simplified accounting, a lane has a `{python} LinkBudgetScenario.budget_db_str` allowance. A `{python} LinkBudgetScenario.cable_m_str` DAC cable\index{DAC!signal attenuation loss} contributing `{python} LinkBudgetScenario.cable_loss_db_str` of loss and connectors contributing `{python} LinkBudgetScenario.connector_loss_db_str` leave `{python} LinkBudgetScenario.margin_db_str` of margin. Higher signaling frequencies increase copper loss, so preserving reach can require more signal conditioning, a different cable, or optics\index{Pluggable optics!rack exit requirement}. Aggregate port speed alone does not determine cable reach; lane rate, channel construction, and active components matter. The design must meet both the signal-quality target and the power budget before the transport layer can rely on the link.

## Level 2 Transport and the Performance Model {#sec-network-fabrics-transport}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Transport section — 175B cluster GPU count
class NetworkTransportClusterRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators, commas=True, label="GPU")
```

Large-scale training requires sustained, synchronized bulk transfers. A single AllReduce across `{python} NetworkTransportClusterRecap.n_gpus_str` forwards every worker's contribution through many links in lockstep. This pattern favors RDMA transport offload, reliable completion, and bounded loss-recovery time. A physically lossless fabric is one way to make that performance predictable, but it is not the only design.

### RDMA and GPUDirect {#sec-network-fabrics-rdma}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Transport — NDR line rate in TCP/RDMA discussion.
class IbNdrTransportRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

A conventional kernel TCP path charges the host for every byte it moves. Interrupt processing, protocol work, and payload copies consume CPU cycles and memory bandwidth that the training process also needs for data loading and preprocessing, and the charge grows with aggregate I/O as many streams or NICs drive a host at `{python} IbNdrTransportRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` link rates. Modern TCP stacks reduce the charge with segmentation offload, receive-side scaling, zero-copy interfaces, and careful non-uniform memory access (NUMA) placement, so a single stream need not exhaust a server's memory bandwidth. They do not remove it, and the contention becomes harder to provision predictably as nodes add NICs.

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-remote-direct-memory-access-rdma .callout-definition title="Remote direct memory access (RDMA)"}

***Remote direct memory access (RDMA)***\index{RDMA!definition}\index{Remote direct memory access|see{RDMA}} is a networking technology that offloads transport processing to network interface hardware, allowing access to registered remote memory without per-transfer kernel processing of the payload.

1.  **Significance**: RDMA can reduce end-to-end message latency from tens of microseconds for a kernel TCP path to low-single-digit microseconds on a tuned fabric, shrinking the fixed startup cost that every message adds to the Fleet Law's communication term $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a conventional kernel TCP path, RDMA offloads transport processing to NIC hardware and permits user-space access to registered memory. The resulting CPU-core and memory-bandwidth savings depend on the host, NIC, I/O path, message size, and software configuration rather than on link rate alone.
3.  **Common pitfall**: RDMA is an access and offload model, not one loss-recovery algorithm. Reliable InfiniBand and RoCE transports detect loss and retransmit [@infiniband2000spec]. Some RNIC generations use the Go-Back-N-style recovery noted with the loss inversion, which makes a drop expensive (@sec-network-fabrics-losslessness quantifies the cost), while other designs support stronger selective recovery or tolerate lossy Ethernet without the link-layer pause mechanism (priority flow control) that many RoCE deployments rely on [@mittal2018irn]. The requirement is reliable completion with a recovery tail that the synchronized workload can tolerate, not a physically lossless Ethernet fabric in every implementation.

:::

RDMA bypasses the kernel data path. Offloading transport logic to the NIC allows applications to read and write registered remote memory without per-message kernel intervention. For ML, GPUDirect RDMA\index{GPUDirect RDMA!accelerator memory},[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass] the path that dense nodes pair with one NIC per GPU (@sec-compute-dense-nodes), extends this principle to accelerator memory [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Within a sending node (@fig-gpudirect-data-path), GPUDirect RDMA routes an $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload (what one participant sends, not the model-wide gradient state) along the solid green peer-to-peer path through the PCIe switch straight to the RDMA NIC, bypassing host memory entirely. Without this direct memory access (DMA) bypass, the dashed gray staging path must first copy $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and subsequently read $\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes out to the NIC, generating roughly $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of redundant host-memory bus traffic. The network still transfers the payload, and the PCIe path may comprise multiple DMA transactions; the optimization removes staging copies rather than collapsing the transfer into one transaction.

[^fn-gpudirect-rdma-bypass]: **GPUDirect RDMA**\index{GPUDirect RDMA!zero-copy}: Introduced by NVIDIA for Kepler-class GPUs and CUDA 5.0, GPUDirect RDMA enables a direct PCIe path between GPU memory and third-party peer devices such as network interfaces [@nvidia2026gpudirectRdma]. Before GPUDirect, every gradient transfer had to stage through host memory, consuming CPU memory bandwidth that competes with data loading. Eliminating this bounce path is one reason overlapping communication with backward-pass computation is feasible at scale.

::: {#fig-gpudirect-data-path data-explore="mechanism-scene" data-explore-key="vol2:fig-gpudirect-data-path" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**GPUDirect RDMA Data Path**: Without GPUDirect (dashed), a sending node first writes the $\PointToPointMessageSize$-byte payload from GPU memory into a registered host-memory buffer and the NIC then reads it back out, about $2\PointToPointMessageSize$ bytes of host-memory traffic per payload. With GPUDirect RDMA (solid), the NIC reads GPU memory directly over the PCIe peer-to-peer path, so the host-memory bounce disappears." fig-alt="A sending node drawn as its board layout: host memory with a registered buffer and the CPU root complex along the top, a wide PCIe switch in the middle, and GPU memory holding an n-byte payload beside the RDMA NIC along the bottom. A solid green path climbs from GPU memory into the PCIe switch and drops straight down to the NIC, which sends to the fabric. A dashed gray path climbs from GPU memory through the switch to the CPU, then into host memory, labeled 1, write n, and back out, labeled 2, read n, before descending through the switch to the NIC; a note under host memory reads about 2n bytes of bus traffic. A key labels the solid path GPUDirect RDMA and the dashed path staged via host memory."}
![](images/svg/gpudirect-data-path.svg)

:::

### InfiniBand and RoCE {#sec-network-fabrics-ib-roce}

GPU clusters commonly choose between two RDMA transport stacks, and the decision is a reliability-versus-operations trade-off. Both stacks must keep switch buffers from overflowing under synchronized bursts, and they do so in different places. InfiniBand uses **credit-based flow control**\index{Credit-based flow control!definition}\index{InfiniBand!credit-based flow control}. Each receiver advertises its free buffer space to the sender at the other end of the link in units called credits, and the sender transmits only into space that has been advertised. A buffer therefore cannot overflow; congestion appears as senders waiting for credits rather than as dropped packets. Ethernet was designed to drop packets when buffers fill, so RoCE deployments that want the same behavior add two mechanisms. Priority flow control (PFC)\index{Priority flow control!link-layer backpressure}\index{PFC|see{Priority flow control}} lets a filling switch port send a PAUSE frame that stops its upstream neighbor for one traffic class, and explicit congestion notification (ECN)\index{ECN!congestion signaling}\index{Explicit congestion notification|see{ECN}} marks packets that pass through a filling queue so that their senders slow down before a pause is needed. InfiniBand thus builds losslessness into the link layer, while RoCE assembles it from switch configuration and end-to-end congestion control (@tbl-network-fabrics-rdma-stacks); @sec-network-fabrics-pfc develops PFC's failure modes.

| **Stack**                                                      | **Fabric behavior**                                                                                                                 | **Operational burden**                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  | **Typical fit**                                                                                     |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| InfiniBand (IB)\index{InfiniBand!credit-based flow control}    | Purpose-built HPC switched fabric [@infiniband2000spec] with credit-based flow control, so losslessness is native at the link layer | a central subnet manager\index{InfiniBand!subnet manager} computes routes, and virtual lanes (VLs)\index{InfiniBand!virtual lane}, separate buffer and credit pools on one link, isolate traffic                                                        | Dedicated training clusters where predictable tail latency outweighs Ethernet ecosystem flexibility |
| **RoCE (RDMA over Converged Ethernet)**\index{RoCE!definition} | RoCEv2 carries RDMA semantics by encapsulating InfiniBand transport headers in UDP/IP packets                                       | PFC-based deployments suppress loss with PFC, ECN, and routing policy\index{RoCEv2!congestion control} [@guo2016rdma; @gangidi2024rdma]; PFC-free designs instead place more burden on end-to-end congestion control and loss recovery [@mittal2018irn] | Multi-vendor Ethernet fleets that can absorb more congestion-control tuning                         |

: **RDMA Transport Stack Trade-Offs**: InfiniBand and RoCE expose RDMA semantics through different operational contracts, one built around native losslessness and the other around Ethernet compatibility. {#tbl-network-fabrics-rdma-stacks tbl-colwidths="[20,30,25,25]"}

The InfiniBand\index{IB|see{InfiniBand}}[^fn-infiniband-protocol-origin] row reflects a protocol heritage that favors hardware-managed losslessness over Ethernet compatibility, and this architectural choice is visible at the protocol boundary. @Fig-ib-roce-stack partitions the protocol stack across user-space, kernel, and hardware bands, contrasting traditional socket overhead against direct verbs hardware offload. The conventional copied TCP/IP path on the left uses two software copies across kernel buffer boundaries and runs the protocol in software. The RDMA stack on the right traces a single amber bypass arrow from the collective communication library (such as the NVIDIA Collective Communications Library, or NCCL) and the user-space **verbs API**\index{Verbs API!definition} straight to the RDMA NIC, which keeps the operating system off the active data path.

[^fn-infiniband-protocol-origin]: [offset=-32mm] **InfiniBand**\index{InfiniBand!origin}: Formed in 1999 from the merger of two competing server I/O standards (Future I/O and NGIO), InfiniBand was originally designed to replace PCI as a general-purpose system interconnect. Its pivot to HPC networking preserved the credit-based, hardware-managed flow control that server I/O demanded, and that heritage is why InfiniBand provides native losslessness without the PFC fragility of Ethernet-based RDMA fabrics.

::: {#fig-ib-roce-stack fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Traditional TCP/IP vs. RDMA Verbs Stacks**: Read each stack top to bottom through the user-space, kernel, and hardware bands. In the illustrated copied TCP/IP socket path (left), a send enters the kernel through a system call, the payload is copied into kernel socket buffers and again toward the NIC's transmit ring, and the CPU runs the transport protocol in software. With RDMA verbs over InfiniBand or RoCEv2 (right), the collective library posts work requests from user space, the kernel stays off the data path, and the RDMA NIC runs the reliable transport in hardware, reading GPU memory directly through GPUDirect instead of staging a host copy." fig-alt="Two panels, each divided by dashed lines into user space, kernel, and hardware bands. Left, TCP/IP sockets: training framework in user space, then socket API, TCP/IP stack, and NIC driver in the kernel, then the Ethernet NIC; beside the stack, three payload tiles marked n attach to the framework, the socket API, and the NIC driver and are labeled user buf, socket buf, and TX ring; dashed arrows labeled copy 1 and copy 2 join them, and a thin solid arrow labeled DMA read carries the TX ring into the Ethernet NIC; the footer reads CPU copies data and runs the transport. Right, RDMA verbs: NCCL above the verbs API in user space, then a single amber arrow straight through the empty kernel band, labeled kernel not on the data path, to the RDMA NIC with transport in hardware; a GPU memory box beside the NIC holds a single payload tile and feeds the NIC through a short green arrow; the footer reads NIC reads GPU memory directly (GPUDirect)."}
![](images/svg/networking-stacks.svg)

:::

### Reliable delivery and loss recovery {#sec-network-fabrics-losslessness}

By routing the user-space verbs API directly to hardware (@fig-ib-roce-stack), the architecture decouples collective library calls from the operating system, leaving the transport hardware and fabric to arbitrate reliable delivery and packet loss. Reliable connected transports in both InfiniBand and RoCE detect loss and retransmit [@infiniband2000spec]; credits and PFC exist to make that retransmission rare [@guo2016rdma; @gangidi2024rdma]. Losslessness is therefore a deployment contract rather than a property of RDMA as a family. Designs that operate over lossy Ethernet without PFC shift more responsibility to endpoint congestion control, packet reordering, and selective recovery [@mittal2018irn].

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Go-Back-N paragraph below — data resent after one drop.
# │ How: resent window = line rate × loss-detection delay; a timeout-based
# │      detection lengthens the delay.
class GoBackNWindow:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    line_rate = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth  # 50 GB/s per direction
    detect_delay = 5 * microsecond  # scenario assumption: same 5 μs feedback round trip as the incast analysis
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    resent = line_rate * detect_delay
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(resent.to(KB).magnitude - 250) < 1e-6, "50 GB/s × 5 μs should be 250 KB")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    line_rate_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(line_rate, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    detect_delay_us_str = fmt_time(detect_delay, microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    resent_kb_str = fmt_memory(resent, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Recovery granularity therefore matters. On an RNIC with **Go-Back-N**\index{Go-Back-N!definition}-style recovery and no out-of-order retention, a lost packet invalidates every packet that arrives after it, and the sender must retransmit from the missing sequence point. The penalty is everything the sender transmitted between the lost packet and the moment it learned of the loss, so it equals link rate times detection delay. If the receiver's negative acknowledgment reaches the sender after one `{python} GoBackNWindow.detect_delay_us_str` round trip, a sender at `{python} GoBackNWindow.line_rate_gb_per_s_str` has meanwhile sent `{python} GoBackNWindow.resent_kb_str`, all of which it must send again; a drop 900 MB into a 1 GB transfer wastes that window, not the 900 MB already delivered. When detection instead waits for a retransmission timeout, the delay, and with it the resent window, grows with that timeout. An RNIC with selective recovery retransmits only the missing packets, so the same physical loss produces a shorter tail [@mittal2018irn]. Because the window is line rate times detection delay, resending it takes about as long as detecting the loss did, so a faster link resends more bytes per drop without shortening the stall. Either way the stall spans many packet wire times, and a synchronous collective exposes the slowest recovery to every waiting worker. Fabric designers can reduce that tail by suppressing drops with PFC, by using a loss-tolerant transport with bounded endpoint recovery, or by combining congestion control and admission policy so queues rarely overflow. Each choice moves state and failure modes between switches and endpoints.

### The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ performance model {#sec-network-fabrics-performance-model}

Protocol choice determines how the fabric provides reliable completion and bounds loss-recovery time; performance modeling then asks how fast it can carry a given message. The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ model\index{Alpha-beta model!message transfer time} (principle \ref{pri-alpha-beta-model}) decomposes message transfer time as $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$, where $\PointToPointMessageSize$ is the message size in bytes, $\MessageStartupLatency$ is the fixed startup latency, and $\LinkBandwidth$ is the sustained bandwidth in bytes per unit time [@hockney1994]. The physical topology influences both parameters through path length and available capacity. A collective built from many sequential rounds of messages pays $\MessageStartupLatency$ once per round, so its startup cost can grow with the number of participants even when the underlying fabric provides short physical paths.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The same decomposition, multiplied by each schedule's round count and traffic factor, is developed for collective algorithms in @sec-communication-collective-operations-collective-operations-network-performance-modeling-0d8e.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-alpha-beta-refactor
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ NETWORK ALPHA-BETA MODEL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-performance-model
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the latency-bandwidth crossover for InfiniBand vs Ethernet.
# │ Show: Crossover points (~75 KB for IB); impact on small vs large messages.
# │ How: T = alpha + n/beta. Small msg: 4 KB; Large msg: 350 MB.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_math, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_percent, fmt_time

class NetworkAlphaBeta:
    """Namespace for the alpha-beta communication model."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ───────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Level 1: Hardware Specs
    FABRIC_ALPHA_NDR = Systems.SwitchFabric.AlphaNdr
    # Scenario parameters, not universal protocol constants. Measured alpha and
    # delivered beta vary with NIC, topology, software, and message placement.
    alpha_ib = FABRIC_ALPHA_NDR
    beta_ib = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth
    eth_alpha = Systems.SwitchFabric.AlphaRoce
    eth_beta = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G.bandwidth

    # Level 2: Messages
    n_small = 4000 * byte  # scenario assumption: 4 KB control message
    n_large = 350 * MB  # scenario assumption: 350 MB gradient shard

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    n_cross_ib = calc_alpha_beta_crossover(alpha_ib, beta_ib)
    n_cross_eth = calc_alpha_beta_crossover(eth_alpha, eth_beta)

    t_small_ib = calc_point_to_point_time(n_small, alpha_ib, beta_ib)
    t_small_eth = calc_point_to_point_time(n_small, eth_alpha, eth_beta)
    small_bw_term_pct = ((n_small / beta_ib) / t_small_ib).to_base_units().magnitude * 100
    small_speedup = (t_small_eth / t_small_ib).to_base_units().magnitude

    # Small-message worked-equation terms (microseconds), for the alpha-beta callout.
    ib_small_xfer_us = (n_small / beta_ib).to(microsecond).magnitude
    eth_small_xfer_us = (n_small / eth_beta).to(microsecond).magnitude

    t_large_ib = calc_point_to_point_time(n_large, alpha_ib, beta_ib)
    t_large_eth = calc_point_to_point_time(n_large, eth_alpha, eth_beta)
    large_speedup = (t_large_eth / t_large_ib).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_cross_ib < 100 * KB, f"Crossover ({n_cross_ib.to(KB).magnitude:.0f} KB) should be < 100 KB for IB")
    check(small_bw_term_pct < 10, f"Small msg should be latency-bound, got {small_bw_term_pct:.1f}% BW share")
    check(3.0 < small_speedup < 4.0, "Small-message speedup should be about 3.4× for IB vs Ethernet")
    check(3.5 < large_speedup < 4.5, "Large-message speedup should be about 4× for IB vs 100G Ethernet")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_cross_ib_kb_str = fmt_memory(n_cross_ib, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_cross_eth_kb_str = fmt_memory(n_cross_eth, unit=KB, precision=1, commas=False)
    t_small_ib_us_str = fmt_time(t_small_ib, microsecond, precision=2, commas=False)
    small_bw_pct_str = fmt_percent(small_bw_term_pct / 100, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    t_large_ib_ms_str = fmt_time(t_large_ib, millisecond, precision=1, commas=False)
    t_large_eth_ms_str = fmt_time(t_large_eth, millisecond, precision=2, commas=False)
    large_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round(large_speedup), precision=0, commas=False)
    ib_alpha_us_str = fmt_time(alpha_ib, microsecond, precision=1, commas=False)
    ib_beta_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(beta_ib, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_small_kb_str = fmt_memory(n_small, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_large_mb_str = fmt_memory(n_large, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    n_large_grad_mb_str = fmt_memory(n_large, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    eth_alpha_us_str = fmt_time(eth_alpha, microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    eth_beta_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(eth_beta, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    eth_beta_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(eth_beta, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    doubled_beta_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(2 * beta_ib, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)

    # Worked small-message equations for the alpha-beta crossover callout.
    _a_ib = alpha_ib.to(microsecond).magnitude
    _b_ib = beta_ib.to(GB / second).magnitude
    _a_eth = eth_alpha.to(microsecond).magnitude
    _b_eth = eth_beta.to(GB / second).magnitude
    _n_kb = n_small.to(KB).magnitude
    small_ib_eq_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{_a_ib:.1f}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{{s}} + {_n_kb:.0f}\,\text{{KB}}/{_b_ib:.0f}\,\text{{GB/s}} "
        rf"= {_a_ib:.1f} + {ib_small_xfer_us:.2f} = \mathbf{{{t_small_ib.to(microsecond).magnitude:.2f}}}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{{s}}"
    )
    small_eth_eq_math = fmt_math(
        rf"{_a_eth:.1f}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{{s}} + {_n_kb:.0f}\,\text{{KB}}/{_b_eth:.1f}\,\text{{GB/s}} "
        rf"= {_a_eth:.1f} + {eth_small_xfer_us:.2f} = \mathbf{{{t_small_eth.to(microsecond).magnitude:.2f}}}\,\MicroUnitPrefix\text{{s}}"
    )
    small_speedup_mult_str = fmt_multiple(small_speedup, precision=1, commas=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: alpha-beta crossover notebook — third path that separates the
# │          transport (alpha) from the line rate (beta).
# │ How: RoCE alpha on a 400 Gb/s Ethernet link, same messages as NetworkAlphaBeta.
class AlphaBetaSameRate:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    alpha = NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_alpha
    beta = Systems.Fabrics.RoCE_400G.bandwidth
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_small = calc_point_to_point_time(NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small, alpha, beta)
    t_large = calc_point_to_point_time(NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large, alpha, beta)
    small_ratio = (t_small / NetworkAlphaBeta.t_small_ib).to_base_units().magnitude
    large_ratio = (t_large / NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_ib).to_base_units().magnitude
    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(beta == NetworkAlphaBeta.beta_ib, "Same-rate path must match the NDR line rate")
    check(small_ratio > 2, "Same-rate RoCE should stay several times slower for small messages")
    check(large_ratio < 1.01, "Same-rate RoCE should match NDR within 1 percent for large messages")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    beta_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(beta, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    t_small_us_str = fmt_time(t_small, microsecond, precision=2, commas=False)
    t_large_ms_str = fmt_time(t_large, millisecond, precision=1, commas=False)
    small_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(small_ratio, precision=1, commas=False)
```

The model reveals two regimes that call for different engineering responses. When $\PointToPointMessageSize< \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth$, the startup cost $\MessageStartupLatency$ exceeds the transmission cost, placing small control messages deep in the latency-bound region, whereas when $\PointToPointMessageSize> \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth$, the $\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$ term dominates and large gradient transfers sit deep in the bandwidth-bound region. Near the crossover both terms matter, and where a collective lands also depends on how its algorithm divides the payload into messages and schedules them across rounds.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The crossover message size that separates the latency-dominated and bandwidth-dominated regimes, with a worked InfiniBand NDR example, is developed in @sec-appdx-comm-foundations-regimes.
:::

For the modeled NDR InfiniBand path with $\MessageStartupLatency=$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_alpha_us_str` and $\LinkBandwidth=$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_beta_gb_per_s_str`, the crossover point $\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\cdot \LinkBandwidth\approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_ib_kb_str`. Measured startup latency and delivered bandwidth vary with the NIC, switch path, software stack, and contention, so these parameters describe a scenario rather than a protocol constant. Far below the crossover, more bandwidth removes only a small part of transfer time; far above it, lower startup latency removes only a small part. Shorter paths can lower $\MessageStartupLatency$, while additional delivered path bandwidth raises $\LinkBandwidth$; their value depends on the message sizes the workload actually exchanges.

::: {#nbk-network-fabrics-alpha-beta-crossover .callout-notebook title="The alpha-beta crossover"}

**Problem**: A fabric designer is comparing a modeled InfiniBand NDR path (`{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_alpha_us_str`, `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_beta_gb_per_s_str`) against a modeled RoCE path over slower Ethernet (`{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_alpha_us_str`, `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_beta_gb_per_s_str`). The comparison deliberately bundles a higher-latency stack with a slower link, so a third path, RoCE on a `{python} AlphaBetaSameRate.beta_gbit_per_s_str` link, separates the two effects. For a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str` control message and a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_mb_str` gradient shard, which part of $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize)=\MessageStartupLatency+\PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$ dominates, and why does the first path help for different reasons in each regime?

**Math**:
Apply $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) = \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth$ for a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str` control message and a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_mb_str` gradient shard.

1. **Small message** (`{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str`):
   - InfiniBand: `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_ib_eq_math`
   - RoCE (100G): `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_eth_eq_math`
   - **Result**: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_speedup_mult_str` faster because its modeled $\MessageStartupLatency$ is lower.
2. **Large message** (`{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_mb_str`):
   - InfiniBand: $\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_ib_ms_str`
   - RoCE (100G): $\PointToPointTransferTime= \MessageStartupLatency+ \PointToPointMessageSize/\LinkBandwidth=$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_eth_ms_str`
   - **Result**: Under these assumed path parameters, the NDR path is `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.large_speedup_mult_str` faster because its modeled $\LinkBandwidth$ is higher. That factor is the ratio of the two line rates, so it measures the faster link rather than the transport.
3. **Same line rate** (RoCE at `{python} AlphaBetaSameRate.beta_gbit_per_s_str`, RoCE $\MessageStartupLatency$):
   - Small message: `{python} AlphaBetaSameRate.t_small_us_str`, still `{python} AlphaBetaSameRate.small_ratio_mult_str` the NDR time, because $\MessageStartupLatency$ alone separates the stacks.
   - Large message: `{python} AlphaBetaSameRate.t_large_ms_str`, essentially the NDR time, because at equal $\LinkBandwidth$ nothing but a few microseconds of $\MessageStartupLatency$ separates them.

**Systems insight**: This scenario places the crossover $(\LatencyBandwidthCrossoverSize = \MessageStartupLatency\LinkBandwidth)$ near `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_ib_kb_str`. Because gradients are megabytes to gigabytes, their transfers are usually bandwidth dominated, whereas pipeline coordination can remain latency dominated\index{Latency!dominated regime}. A higher line rate produces little benefit for a message whose startup term dominates; transport processing, topology, and hop count then govern the improvement.

:::

In the 175B training job, a `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_small_kb_str` control message, such as the notification that tells a pipeline stage its next microbatch is ready, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_small_ib_us_str`, with bandwidth contributing only `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.small_bw_pct_str` of the total. Faster links therefore offer little benefit for this handoff. A `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_large_grad_mb_str` gradient shard, roughly the share of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient that each of the `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.n_gpus_str` owns when a reduction partitions it across the whole cluster, costs $\PointToPointTransferTime(\PointToPointMessageSize) \approx$ `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.t_large_ib_ms_str`; doubling bandwidth to `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.doubled_beta_gb_per_s_str` would approximately halve its transfer time.

Across the full range of message sizes, each path traces a flat latency-dominated plateau that bends into a linear bandwidth-dominated regime (@fig-alpha-beta-crossover). On the modeled NDR path, the knee at `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_ib_kb_str` marks where transmission time overtakes the `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.ib_alpha_us_str` startup latency; the `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_beta_gbit_per_s_str` RoCE path sits on a higher floor of `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.eth_alpha_us_str` and bends near `{python} NetworkAlphaBeta.n_cross_eth_kb_str`. The exact positions reflect the assumed $\MessageStartupLatency$ and $\LinkBandwidth$ scenario parameters rather than invariant protocol constants. On both paths, startup latency governs sub-kilobyte control handoffs, whereas multi-megabyte gradient shards sit well inside the bandwidth-bound regime.

::: {#fig-alpha-beta-crossover fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The $\MessageStartupLatency$-$\LinkBandwidth$ Crossover**: Modeled transfer time as a function of message size for an NDR InfiniBand path and a 100 Gb/s RoCE baseline using the scenario parameters in the text. Small messages are latency dominated (flat region), while large messages are bandwidth dominated (linear region); on the InfiniBand path the dotted asymptotes show the knee sitting where the two terms are equal. Measured crossover points vary with the end-to-end path." fig-alt="Log-log modeled transfer time vs. message size for one NDR InfiniBand scenario and one 100 gigabit per second RoCE scenario, with each crossover point marked by a dot and a label giving its message size, and latency-dominated and bandwidth-dominated regions labeled. Each series is labeled with its startup latency and bandwidth, the Ethernet label above its plateau and the InfiniBand label below. For the InfiniBand path, two dotted asymptotes, a horizontal startup floor alpha and a diagonal transmission line n over beta, meet directly beneath its crossover point."}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ ALPHA-BETA CROSSOVER (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-alpha-beta-crossover—latency vs bandwidth regime in fabric
# │          selection
# │
# │ Goal: Visualize transfer time vs message size for InfiniBand NDR vs Ethernet
# │       RoCE; show latency-dominated (flat) vs bandwidth-dominated (linear).
# │ Show: Log-log plot with crossover points (~75 KB for IB); alpha/beta model.
# │ How: T = alpha + n/beta; plot for both fabrics; annotate crossover.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ┌── 1. CANVAS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Visualize transfer time vs message size for InfiniBand NDR vs Ethernet
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.ticker as ticker
import numpy as np
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_bandwidth, fmt_memory

# ┌── 2. ARRAYS ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
alpha_ib_q = Systems.SwitchFabric.AlphaNdr
beta_ib_q = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth
alpha_eth_q = Systems.SwitchFabric.AlphaRoce
beta_eth_q = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_100G.bandwidth

alpha_ib = alpha_ib_q.to(second).magnitude
beta_ib = beta_ib_q.to(byte / second).magnitude
alpha_eth = alpha_eth_q.to(second).magnitude
beta_eth = beta_eth_q.to(byte / second).magnitude

n = np.logspace(0, 10, 1000)
t_ib = np.array([calc_point_to_point_time(size * byte, alpha_ib_q, beta_ib_q).to(second).magnitude for size in n])
t_eth = np.array([calc_point_to_point_time(size * byte, alpha_eth_q, beta_eth_q).to(second).magnitude for size in n])

n_cross_ib_q = calc_alpha_beta_crossover(alpha_ib_q, beta_ib_q)
n_cross_ib = n_cross_ib_q.to(byte).magnitude
t_cross_ib = 2 * alpha_ib
n_cross_eth_q = calc_alpha_beta_crossover(alpha_eth_q, beta_eth_q)
n_cross_eth = n_cross_eth_q.to(byte).magnitude
t_cross_eth = 2 * alpha_eth

fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6, 4.2))

# ┌── 3. RENDER ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Both curves are network paths, so they take the chapter's network encoding
# (@fig-network-bandwidth-scaling): InfiniBand violet dashed with a hollow
# marker, Ethernet solid in the documented TIME slate (figure-visual-language §2.1).
SLATE_TIME = "#5E6B73"  # time/latency slate, same value as the margin-device TIME constant

_c_ib = COLORS['VioletLine']
_c_eth = SLATE_TIME
ib_beta_label = fmt_bandwidth(beta_ib_q, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
eth_beta_label = fmt_bandwidth(beta_eth_q, unit=GB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
ax.plot(n, t_ib, color=_c_ib, linewidth=2.0, linestyle='--')
ax.plot(n, t_eth, color=_c_eth, linewidth=2.0)

# Knee markers: a dot on each curve (hollow for InfiniBand, as in the scaling
# figure); the crossover sizes are given in the adjacent labels.
ax.scatter([n_cross_ib], [t_cross_ib], s=40, zorder=5, facecolors='white', edgecolors=_c_ib, linewidths=1.5)
ax.scatter([n_cross_eth], [t_cross_eth], s=40, zorder=5, color=_c_eth, edgecolors='white', linewidths=1.2)

# The mechanism of the knee, drawn on the InfiniBand path: the two asymptotes of
# T = alpha + n/beta (the startup floor and the transmission line) meet at the
# crossover size, directly beneath the knee marker (where the curve sits at
# 2*alpha). The floor starts just left of the knee so it does not sit on top of
# the dashed plateau; each asymptote is labeled at its far end.
_FS = 11
_n_flat = np.array([n_cross_ib / 40, n_cross_ib * 30])
ax.plot(_n_flat, [alpha_ib, alpha_ib], color=_c_ib, lw=1.1, ls=':', zorder=3)
_n_diag = np.array([alpha_ib * beta_ib / 14, alpha_ib * beta_ib * 8])
ax.plot(_n_diag, _n_diag / beta_ib, color=_c_ib, lw=1.1, ls=':', zorder=3)
ax.text(_n_flat[1] * 1.25, alpha_ib, r'startup floor $\alpha$', color=_c_ib, fontsize=_FS, ha='left', va='center')
ax.text(
    _n_diag[0] / 1.3,
    _n_diag[0] / beta_ib,
    r'transmission $n/\beta$',
    color=_c_ib,
    fontsize=_FS,
    ha='right',
    va='center',
    bbox=dict(facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', pad=1.0),
)

# ┌── 4. DECORATE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# Series labels sit on the open side of each latency plateau (Ethernet above,
# InfiniBand below), backed by a borderless white box so no gridline passes
# through them; crossover values sit beside the knees, clear of the asymptotes.
_lbl_bg = dict(facecolor='white', edgecolor='none', pad=1.0)
ax.text(
    3,
    alpha_ib / 2.6,
    f'InfiniBand NDR\n({alpha_ib*1e6:.1f} µs, {ib_beta_label})',
    color=_c_ib,
    fontsize=_FS,
    fontweight='bold',
    ha='left',
    va='center',
    linespacing=1.1,
    bbox=_lbl_bg,
)
ax.text(
    3,
    alpha_eth * 3.0,
    f'Ethernet RoCE\n({alpha_eth*1e6:.1f} µs, {eth_beta_label})',
    color=_c_eth,
    fontsize=_FS,
    fontweight='bold',
    ha='left',
    va='center',
    linespacing=1.1,
    bbox=_lbl_bg,
)
ax.text(
    n_cross_ib * 1.4,
    alpha_ib / 3.0,
    f'crossover ~{fmt_memory(n_cross_ib_q, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)}',
    color=_c_ib,
    fontsize=_FS,
    ha='left',
    va='center',
)
ax.text(
    n_cross_eth * 1.05,
    t_cross_eth * 5.5,
    f'crossover ~{fmt_memory(n_cross_eth_q, unit=KB, precision=1, commas=False)}',
    color=_c_eth,
    fontsize=_FS,
    ha='right',
    va='center',
)

ax.text(3, 2e-4, "latency dominated", fontsize=_FS, color=COLORS['primary'], ha='left', va='center', style='italic')
ax.text(1e8, 2e-5, "bandwidth dominated", fontsize=_FS, color=COLORS['primary'], ha='center', va='center', style='italic')

ax.set_xscale('log')
ax.set_yscale('log')
ax.set_xlim(1, 1e10)
ax.set_ylim(3e-8, 1)
ax.grid(True, which="major")
ax.grid(False, which="minor")
ax.set_xlabel('Message size (bytes)', fontsize=_FS)
ax.set_ylabel('Transfer time (s)', fontsize=_FS)
ax.tick_params(labelsize=11)
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(ticker.LogLocator(base=10.0, numticks=12))
for _s in ("top", "right"):
```
