### Optical circuit switching and reconfigurable topology {#sec-network-fabrics-ocs}

Every topology so far is fixed when the fabric is cabled, and its switching is electrical. In clusters spanning tens of thousands of accelerators, multi-tier Clos networks, the switched leaf-and-spine family whose full-bisection form is the fat-tree of @sec-network-fabrics-fat-tree, connect groups of endpoints through successive tiers of electrical packet switches. These switches inspect each packet and choose an outgoing link; the alternative considered here changes the physical connections between groups for a longer-lived workload allocation. Every network hop incurs an Optical-Electrical-Optical (OEO) conversion\index{Optical-electrical-optical conversion!power overhead}: incoming photons hit a photodiode, high-speed SerDes circuits deserialize the electrical signal, switch ASICs buffer and route packets across crossbars, and output SerDes drive lasers to re-transmit light over optical fiber.

At 800 Gb/s and 1.6 Tb/s per-port data rates, SerDes and transceiver electronics consume significant energy (@sec-network-fabrics-serdes), and every additional switch tier repeats that conversion cost for each bit that crosses it. Fixed electrical Clos topologies are also cabled statically, locking the facility into a single oversubscription ratio and rigid bisection pattern regardless of whether the running workload is pipeline-dominated, data-parallel, or AllToAll expert-routed. A statically cabled torus is equally fixed. It suits the dimension-ordered rings described in @sec-network-fabrics-dragonfly but congests under MoE AllToAll traffic, and its wiring cannot change to match the job.

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-optical-circuit-switching .callout-definition title="Optical circuit switching"}

***Optical circuit switching (OCS)***\index{Optical circuit switching!definition}\index{OCS!reconfigurable topology} is a physical networking architecture that routes optical signals directly using Micro-Electro-Mechanical Systems (MEMS) mirror arrays without Optical-Electrical-Optical (OEO) conversion, enabling dynamic, software-defined topology reconfiguration and high energy efficiency at warehouse scale.

1.  **Significance**: An optical circuit bypasses packet-by-packet electronic processing in the switching path. The complete system still consumes power for actuators, control, and transceivers. Its compatibility across line rates depends on optical loss, wavelengths, and endpoint budgets, so protocol transparency does not imply unrestricted upgrades.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike electrical packet switches (which inspect headers, buffer packets in SRAM, and make nanosecond routing decisions per packet), an OCS establishes semi-static physical optical circuits with millisecond-scale switching latency ($10$--$30$ ms), making it suitable for topology-level reconfiguration rather than dynamic packet routing.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming OCS replaces packet switching entirely. OCS operates at circuit granularity: it configures cluster-scale topologies (such as 3D tori or job-specific sub-clusters) and routes around hardware faults, while packet switching or accelerator-native interconnects handle fine-grained, intra-step message routing.

:::

Google's TPU v4 supercomputer [@jouppi2023] deployed optical circuit switching in production. Instead of wiring 4,096 chips into an inflexible electrical fat-tree, the system groups accelerators into $4{\times}4{\times}4$ node cubes and routes the inter-cube links through an array of 3D MEMS optical circuit switches (codenamed Palomar)\index{Optical circuit switching!MEMS mirror array}.

The optical layer serves two purposes, adapting the topology to the workload and recovering from faults. For workload adaptation, the physical interconnect can be reconfigured\index{Optical circuit switching!topology reconfiguration} to match the communication structure of the running model. A training run using 1D pipeline parallelism can configure its slice as an elongated cylinder to streamline stage-to-stage transfers. Conversely, a 2D or 3D tensor-parallel partition can configure a compact cubic 3D torus that minimizes average hop count, while an MoE workload can maximize bisection bandwidth across specific expert groups.

Optical switching also supports fault isolation\index{Optical circuit switching!fault isolation} by changing connections around unavailable hardware where spare connectivity permits. The capability matters because in a statically cabled torus, a single failed link or node can break a ring along an entire dimension and degrade every job that spans it. With optical circuit switching, the mirrors can be redirected to bypass the failed cube or fiber and splice healthy cubes into a complete, smaller torus slice without manual recabling. The fabric manager must first detect the fault, choose a feasible allocation, and establish the new circuits, which means circuit-switching time is only one part of recovery; a training job may also need to rebuild its process groups and restore state before computation resumes, so optical reconfiguration latency alone does not specify recovery time.

The trade-off is switching latency. Because MEMS mirrors physically rotate to steer collimated light beams, reconfiguration occurs on a mechanical timescale that is much longer than packet forwarding in an established electrical path. Circuit setup changes connectivity, while packet forwarding uses connectivity already in place. Consequently, OCS raises the power and protocol ceiling of the switching layer while leaving reconfiguration latency as the binding constraint, so it is deployed for job-level topology allocation and fault isolation, not for per-message dynamic routing. Within that limit, OCS turns the choice of topology from a decision fixed when the fabric is cabled into one made for each job.

Each topology comparison so far has considered one traffic pattern at a time. In practice, clusters serve multiple workloads with different communication patterns, and topology selection must balance their competing demands.

::: {#chk-network-fabrics-topology-selection-your-workload .callout-checkpoint title="Topology selection for your workload"}

The choice of network topology dictates the upper bound of training efficiency. Warm up by matching each single-workload pattern to its ideal topology, then design a fabric that must serve several at once.

**Single-workload picks**

- [ ] **AllReduce bandwidth**: select the topology that maximizes $\BisectionBandwidth$ for a standard data-parallel job dominated by AllReduce.
- [ ] **MoE traffic**: select the topology that best sustains a mixture-of-experts model's AllToAll-dominant, bursty communication, in which any rank may send to any other.
- [ ] **Neighbor locality**: select the topology that best fits a ring AllReduce scheduled along each dimension of the machine, where every transfer goes to a physical neighbor.

**Designing for a mixed cluster**

You are designing the network for a new ML cluster that will run two primary workloads: (1) training a 175B-parameter language model using 3D parallelism (tensor, pipeline, and data parallelism), and (2) serving a mixture-of-experts model that relies heavily on AllToAll communication to route tokens to the correct experts.

- [ ] **Training topology**: select the topology (fat-tree, rail-optimized, or hybrid) that best matches tensor parallelism within groups of 8 GPUs and data parallelism across all nodes, then justify the choice.
- [ ] **MoE topology**: revise the topology choice for unpredictable AllToAll traffic where any GPU may need to communicate with any other GPU.
- [ ] **Oversubscription risk**: identify which workload suffers more under 2:1 spine-layer oversubscription and propose a scheduling strategy to mitigate the impact.

:::

class NetworkFabricBridgeRecap:

Topology provides the structural capacity for the cluster of `{python} NetworkFabricBridgeRecap.n_gpus_str` to communicate, but structure alone does not guarantee performance. When the `{python} NetworkFabricBridgeRecap.n_gpus_str` synchronize contributions to the model's `{python} NetworkRunningExampleCluster.grad_gb_str` gradient state, that theoretical capacity collides with the reality of **fabric behavior**\index{Fabric behavior!definition}: congestion control and routing dynamics determine whether this traffic flows smoothly or gridlocks under the strict synchronization of the BSP model.

## Level 4 Fabric Behavior, Congestion, and Routing {#sec-network-fabrics-behavior}

A collective can finish late even when the topology provides full $\BisectionBandwidth$. Levels 1 through 3 determine how long a transfer takes on an unloaded path; fabric behavior determines how much longer it takes once the job's own synchronized traffic loads that path. Competing flows can concentrate on one output path, and the BSP barrier introduced in @sec-network-workload-inversion exposes any delay that extends the last required transfer. The relevant paths are those used by the participating workers; a congested link elsewhere in the fleet need not affect the job. In the Fleet Law (@eq-fleet-law), measured transfer durations contribute to $\CommunicationTime(\DeviceCount)$, while residual waiting at synchronization contributes to $\SynchronizationTime(\DeviceCount)$, the point where the communication axis of C³ hands its cost to the coordination axis. A timeline must assign each interval consistently so the same congestion delay is not counted twice.

The p99 tail latency introduced with the BSP barrier helps expose delays that an average hides, but a particular barrier waits for its last required participant, not for a percentile. Evaluating a fabric therefore requires both transfer-time distributions and the collective completion times they produce under load.

### Priority flow control (PFC) {#sec-network-fabrics-pfc}

The BSP weakest-link property means that even a single dropped packet can trigger a retransmission timeout that stalls the global barrier for milliseconds, a delay that can rival the entire communication phase of a training step. PFC-based RoCEv2 fabrics prevent the drop in the first place by running PFC\index{Priority flow control!lossless mode}, the pause mechanism introduced with the RDMA stacks (@sec-network-fabrics-ib-roce), in lossless mode, so that upstream senders stop before any buffer saturates [@guo2016rdma; @gangidi2024rdma].

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-priority-flow-control .callout-definition title="Priority flow control"}

***Priority flow control (PFC)***\index{Priority flow control!definition} is a link-layer mechanism used by RoCEv2 ML cluster fabrics to prevent switch buffer overflow. When a port's queue depth crosses a configured threshold, the switch sends PAUSE frames to an upstream sender, which throttles injection on a per-priority basis without dropping packets.

1.  **Significance**: In PFC-based RoCEv2 deployments, PFC is the foundation for a lossless Ethernet service. A PFC PAUSE frame must reach the upstream sender before the buffer overflows, so each pause threshold must leave headroom for the data still in flight during roughly one link round trip.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike standard IEEE 802.3 flow control, which pauses all traffic classes on a link, PFC operates per priority class, allowing latency-sensitive control messages to continue flowing while only pausing the congested gradient data queue.
3.  **Common pitfall**: A frequent misconception is that PFC solves congestion. It transforms packet loss into congestion spreading. PFC itself places no bound on how far PAUSE frames propagate, so a single faulty transceiver can pause traffic far from its own link unless a watchdog intervenes.

:::

The danger of PFC lies in its cascading nature\index{Priority flow control!cascading PAUSE frames}. When a switch port's buffer fills, it sends a PAUSE frame upstream, which can move congestion into the upstream switch and trigger another PAUSE frame. A slow receiver, routing hot spot, or true fan-in burst can therefore pause links unrelated to the original queue. This behavior, known as **congestion spreading**\index{Congestion spreading!definition}, is the primary operational risk of PFC-based lossless Ethernet, and the flows it stalls without ever touching the congested queue are called **victim flows**\index{Victim flow!definition}. Fan-in is one trigger, but it is not intrinsic to every collective. A bandwidth-optimal ring exchanges data point to point, although multiple ring flows can still collide at a shared egress or an oversubscribed cut and create a hot spot without a single aggregation receiver (@sec-network-fabrics-incast).

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/network_fabrics_pfc_pause_blast.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Three columns labeled senders, switches, and full port. A red square on the right sends three dashed red arrows marked PAUSE leftward to three violet switch squares, and each switch sends two lighter dashed red arrows leftward to two blue sender dots."}

*PAUSE frames climb back tier by tier and stall senders far from the full port.*
:::

### Lossless fabric hazards and watchdog recovery {#sec-network-pfc-hazards}

While priority flow control provides the illusion of a lossless physical layer, relying on link-layer backpressure introduces structural failure modes that do not exist in loss-tolerant packet-switched networks. When switch queues cannot drop packets to relieve congestion, pressure propagates backward through the network graph, creating two distinct hyperscale failure modes: buffer-dependency deadlocks and PFC storms.

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-pfc-deadlock .callout-definition title="Cyclic buffer dependency deadlock"}

***Cyclic buffer dependency deadlock***\index{PFC deadlock!definition}\index{Cyclic buffer dependency!definition} is a permanent distributed lockup in a lossless network, whether its backpressure uses PFC PAUSE frames or InfiniBand credits. A set of switch port queues forms a closed dependency cycle, and each queue holds packets destined for the next queue while backpressure from that same queue pauses it.

1.  **Significance**: A single such deadlock permanently halts traffic across all participating ports and upstream links, requiring manual intervention or watchdog timeouts that discard packets to recover. InfiniBand fabrics prevent it through deadlock-free routing and virtual-lane assignment, and PFC-based Ethernet fabrics need the same discipline in their routing and priority configuration.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike a PFC storm (which is a transient cascade of backpressure triggered by a slow-draining endpoint), a buffer-dependency deadlock is a static, self-sustaining topological cycle that cannot resolve itself even after traffic injection stops.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Assuming multi-stage Clos (fat-tree) fabrics are inherently immune to deadlocks. Dynamic multipath routing, link failures, and address resolution flooding can introduce cyclic forwarding dependencies across switch tiers.

:::

#### The graph mechanics of buffer-dependency deadlocks {#sec-network-deadlock-graph}

In a lossless network, a switch cannot forward a packet to downstream buffer $\PacketBuffer_j$ if $\PacketBuffer_j$ is full; instead, it holds the packet in upstream buffer $\PacketBuffer_i$ and awaits credit or pause clearance. A directed buffer dependency graph $\BufferDependencyGraph= (\BufferDependencyVertexSet, \BufferDependencyEdgeSet)$ formalizes this relationship. Each vertex $\PacketBuffer_k \in \BufferDependencyVertexSet$ represents a packet buffer or virtual lane queue at a switch port. A directed edge $(\PacketBuffer_i, \PacketBuffer_j) \in \BufferDependencyEdgeSet$ indicates that a packet currently occupying buffer $\PacketBuffer_i$ requires buffer $\PacketBuffer_j$ along its routing path to make forward progress.

A directed cycle in the buffer dependency graph is a necessary condition for a cyclic buffer dependency deadlock (definition \ref{dfn-network-fabrics-pfc-deadlock}), but a cycle alone does not establish that progress has stopped. The cyclic dependency in @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle becomes a deadlock when the occupied buffers cannot drain and every participant waits for its successor:

$$\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \dots \to \PacketBuffer_k \to \PacketBuffer_1$$ {#eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle}

When each buffer in the cycle fills beyond its configured pause threshold, each port asserts a PFC PAUSE frame to its predecessor. Because no buffer can advance a packet into a paused successor, no buffer can drain, and no port can de-assert its PAUSE signal. The entire cycle freezes permanently. A four-switch ring whose queues ($\PacketBuffer_1$ through $\PacketBuffer_4$) are completely full shows this mutual protocol interlock (@fig-pfc-credit-deadlock). Solid gray arrows trace packet forwarding dependencies advancing clockwise ($\PacketBuffer_1 \to \PacketBuffer_2 \to \PacketBuffer_3 \to \PacketBuffer_4 \to \PacketBuffer_1$), while dashed red PAUSE frames propagate counterclockwise. Each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while waiting for its downstream successor to drain, permanently freezing all four queues until an external watchdog intervenes to drop frames.

::: {#fig-pfc-credit-deadlock data-explore="mechanism-scene" data-explore-key="vol2:fig-pfc-credit-deadlock" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A PFC Deadlock from a Cyclic Buffer Dependency**: Four switch queues form the cycle of @eq-network-buffer-dependency-cycle. Follow the solid arrows clockwise: each full buffer holds packets that need space in the next. The dashed PAUSE frames run counterclockwise, so each full queue pauses its upstream predecessor while awaiting space in its downstream successor, and no queue can drain until a watchdog drops packets." fig-alt="Four switch boxes arranged as a ring, switch 1 at the top, 2 at the right, 3 at the bottom, and 4 at the left, each containing a full red four-slot queue labeled b1 to b4 and the words queue full. Solid dark arrows curve clockwise around the outside of the ring from switch 1 to 2 to 3 to 4 and back to 1, labeled b1 to b2, b2 to b3, b3 to b4, and b4 to b1. Dashed red arrows labeled PAUSE curve counterclockwise around the inside of the ring between the same switches, and the center of the ring reads deadlock."}
![](images/svg/pfc-credit-deadlock.svg)
:::

Routing changes and flooding can create the dependencies needed for deadlock. During link failure or Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) convergence, inconsistent forwarding tables can create transient loops. A lossy IP network eventually discards a looping packet when its time-to-live expires; a lossless class has no such release, so looping traffic can fill the buffers along the loop and hold them. If traffic occupies a cycle of mutually blocked queues, backpressure can prevent progress until recovery breaks the dependency. Multicast or broadcast replication can also fill queues whose dependencies intersect, while cross-connects and asymmetric failover paths can introduce cycles absent from the intended hierarchical route. None of these conditions alone proves a deadlock; the occupied buffers and pause states must form the closed waiting cycle described by the model. Microsoft's production RoCE deployment encountered the flooding trigger directly (war story \ref{ws-network-fabrics-microsoft-pfc-deadlock}).

::: {#ws-network-fabrics-microsoft-pfc-deadlock .callout-war-story title="Microsoft's PFC deadlock (2016)"}

**Context**: A team led by Chuanxiong Guo at Microsoft Research deployed RoCEv2 across Microsoft's data centers, a fleet operating at the scale of tens of thousands of servers, to support latency-sensitive services. Their design provided a lossless fabric with PFC, and the team developed a Differentiated Services Code Point (DSCP)-based PFC mechanism to extend the deployment beyond virtual local area network (VLAN) boundaries [@guo2016rdma].

**Mechanism**: PFC interacted with Ethernet flooding to create a cyclic buffer dependency. A dead server with an incomplete mapping between an IP address and a media-access-control address caused upstream switches to flood lossless packets to every port; PFC PAUSE frames then propagated upstream in response to the flooded traffic, forming a closed loop of paused buffers.

**Impact**: Lossless traffic through the switches in the cycle stopped entirely and stayed stopped, because no buffer in the dependency loop could drain without outside intervention.

**Fix**: Microsoft blocked broadcast and multicast traffic from entering lossless traffic classes, and dropped lossless packets when the corresponding Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) entry was incomplete rather than falling back to flooding.

**Systems lesson**: PFC backpressure is a structural vulnerability of lossless Ethernet at hyperscale. RoCE fabrics require packet-class discipline, PFC pause telemetry, and hardware-level safeguards because a mechanism designed to avoid packet loss can itself become the failure mode. ML training fabrics built on RoCE inherit this risk directly. A single incomplete ARP entry can freeze the lossless class that carries a multi-thousand-GPU training run's gradients, with the cluster appearing healthy while no gradient flows between workers.

:::

#### PFC storms and victim flows {#sec-network-pfc-storms}

In contrast to a static topological cycle, a **PFC storm**\index{PFC storm!definition} is a dynamic, runaway amplification phenomenon triggered when a single "slow drainer" (an accelerator stalled by memory bus saturation, operating system preemption, or a degraded transceiver with elevated bit error rates) fails to consume packets at wire speed. The attached ToR switch queue fills and sends a PAUSE frame to the sender. Because multi-port switches aggregate traffic from many sources across shared packet buffers, the paused queue blocks buffer allocation for unrelated packets (head-of-line blocking). The spine switches feeding that ToR then fill their buffers and pause the other leaf switches that send through them, and each additional tier widens the set of paused links until traffic between node pairs that never communicated with the stalled worker also stops. These victim flows\index{Victim flow!PFC cascade} turn one slow endpoint into a job-wide barrier delay, because every data-parallel worker whose path crosses a paused spine port now arrives late at the barrier. Because a degraded transceiver is one such slow drainer, a component-exposure calculation shows how often a cluster should expect at least one, even though exposure alone does not estimate the probability of a PFC storm.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: transceiver-degradation-probability
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ TRANSCEIVER DEGRADATION PROBABILITY (NOTEBOOK)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: "Probability of at least one transceiver degradation" notebook
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify component-degradation exposure in a large RoCE cluster.
# │ Show: probability of at least one degradation ≈ 22%.
# │ How: Pr(any degradation) = 1 - (1 - p)^N_transceivers.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_percent

class TransceiverDegradationRisk:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = 4096  # scenario assumption: large RoCE cluster size
    links_per_gpu = 3  # scenario assumption: leaf + spine + core link tiers per GPU
    transceivers_per_link = 2  # one module at each end of an optical link
    p_transceiver_degrade = 1e-5  # scenario assumption: 0.001 percent per transceiver per day
    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────
    n_total_links = n_gpus * links_per_gpu
    n_total_transceivers = n_total_links * transceivers_per_link
    p_no_degradation = (1 - p_transceiver_degrade) ** n_total_transceivers
    p_any_degradation = 1 - p_no_degradation
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ─────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_total_links == 12288, f"Total links {n_total_links} outside expected range")
    check(n_total_transceivers == 24576, f"Total transceivers {n_total_transceivers} outside expected range")
    check(0.2 < p_any_degradation < 0.23, f"Degradation probability {p_any_degradation:.2f} outside expected range")
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_int(n_gpus, commas=False)
    p_degrade_pct_str = fmt_percent(
        p_transceiver_degrade,
        precision=3,
        commas=False,
        style="prose",
    )
    total_links_str = fmt(n_total_links, precision=0)
    total_transceivers_str = fmt(n_total_transceivers, precision=0)
    no_degradation_prob_str = fmt(p_no_degradation, precision=3, commas=False)
    any_degradation_prob_decimal_str = fmt(p_any_degradation, precision=3, commas=False)
    any_degradation_prob_str = fmt_percent(p_any_degradation, precision=1, commas=False, style='prose')
    no_degradation_prob_math = fmt_math(
        f"\\Pr(\\text{{no degradation}}) = (1 - 0.00001)^{{{total_transceivers_str}}} " f"\\approx {no_degradation_prob_str}"
    )
    any_degradation_prob_math = fmt_math(
        f"\\Pr(\\text{{at least one degradation}}) = 1 - {no_degradation_prob_str} " f"= \\mathbf{{{any_degradation_prob_decimal_str}}}"
    )
    links_per_gpu_str = fmt_count(links_per_gpu, commas=False, label="link tier")
```

::: {#nbk-network-fabrics-probability-transceiver-degradation .callout-notebook title="Probability of at least one transceiver degradation"}

**Problem**: A `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.n_gpus_str`-GPU RoCE cluster, larger than the reference cluster, is in operation. If the probability that a given transceiver begins degrading on a given day is `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.p_degrade_pct_str`, what is the chance that at least one transceiver degrades on a given day?

**Math**:
Assume independent transceiver-degradation events with the same per-device probability.

1. **Total exposure**: `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.n_gpus_str` $\times$ `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.links_per_gpu_str` = `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.total_links_str` links, or `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.total_transceivers_str` transceivers.
2. **Probability of zero transceiver degradations**: `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.no_degradation_prob_math`.
3. **Probability of at least one degradation**: `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.any_degradation_prob_math` (about `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.any_degradation_prob_str`).

**Systems insight**: Under these assumptions, a large RoCE cluster has a `{python} TransceiverDegradationRisk.any_degradation_prob_str` daily chance of at least one degraded transceiver. This result motivates hardware telemetry and automated remediation, but estimating fabric-wide freeze risk additionally requires the conditional probability that a degradation triggers and propagates a PFC storm.

:::

#### Watchdog recovery and the lossy alternative {#sec-network-pfc-watchdogs-and-lossy}

Switches can use **PFC watchdog timers**\index{PFC watchdog!definition} to detect prolonged pause states and trigger recovery without a full reboot. The configured threshold $\PfcWatchdogTimeout$ must fit the deployment's pause and recovery budgets; a range such as $50\text{--}200\text{ ms}$ is a configuration example, not a universal requirement. Exceeding it indicates stalled progress, not proof of a cyclic deadlock. Depending on the implementation, mitigation can disable pause handling or discard affected traffic so blocked queues can drain. The transport must then recover any lost data, with the completion penalty determined by retransmission behavior, outstanding traffic, and the collective's dependencies. On an RNIC with Go-Back-N-style recovery (@sec-network-fabrics-losslessness), each discarded packet also costs the in-flight window behind it, so breaking a pause converts a stalled queue into a retransmission tail that the waiting collective absorbs.

This systemic brittleness is driving hyperscale operators toward next-generation architectures such as the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) [@ultraEthernet2025specification], detailed in @sec-network-fabrics-protocol-convergence, and loss-tolerant RDMA designs [@mittal2018irn]. Designs that combine packet spraying\index{Packet spraying!deadlock prevention} with congestion control and selective retransmission can operate without link-layer PFC. Removing PFC removes its pause-based deadlocks and storms, but endpoint recovery must still bound the completion-time penalty of congestion and loss.

### End-to-end congestion control with DCQCN and HPCC {#sec-network-fabrics-congestion-control}

End-to-end congestion control adjusts injection rates before queues reach their pause or overflow thresholds. For a BSP workload with a completion-time target, this is a *latency requirement* rather than an *optional throughput optimization*. Delaying a required transfer can extend the synchronization boundary, so the controller must balance delivered throughput against queueing and recovery tails.

The first widely deployed solution, **DCQCN**\index{DCQCN!definition},[^fn-dcqcn-roce-congestion] operates as a reactive feedback loop using ECN\index{ECN!marking threshold}\index{ECN!CNP feedback loop} [@zhu2015]. When a switch's queue depth exceeds a configured threshold, it marks the ECN bit in the packet header. The receiver echoes this mark back to the sender via a congestion notification packet (CNP), prompting the sender to reduce its injection rate using a multiplicative-decrease algorithm. DCQCN is widely supported, but production AI collectives expose a tuning problem. ECN thresholds and NIC firmware behavior can trade off PFC avoidance, throughput, visibility, and tail latency rather than offering one stable optimum [@gangidi2024rdma].

**HPCC**\index{HPCC!definition}[^fn-hpcc-telemetry-congestion] uses in-network telemetry (INT)\index{In-network telemetry!HPCC} to give the sender more information about path load [@li2019]. Switch measurements of queue occupancy and transmitted traffic let the controller estimate an appropriate injection rate rather than react only to a binary congestion mark. That information still arrives after a feedback delay, so the controller must account for changing load and avoid overreaction. The evaluated design reduces queue buildup and tail latency, but requires switch telemetry support and compatible endpoint processing. DCQCN needs less detailed switch feedback, trading that simpler deployment requirement against a different tuning problem.

[^fn-dcqcn-roce-congestion]: **DCQCN (data center quantized congestion notification)**\index{DCQCN!congestion control}: Introduced by @zhu2015 (Microsoft and Mellanox) at SIGCOMM 2015 for large-scale RDMA fabrics, its binary ECN/CNP feedback loop is simpler to deploy than telemetry-rich schemes. However, it creates a delicate tuning surface for training collectives: Meta's 2024 RoCE deployment showed that aggressive ECN marking\index{ECN!tuning sensitivity} reduces PFC pauses but degrades collective completion time [@gangidi2024rdma].

[^fn-hpcc-telemetry-congestion]: **HPCC (high precision congestion control)**\index{HPCC!congestion control}: Introduced by @li2019 (Alibaba) at SIGCOMM 2019, HPCC requires programmable switch ASICs that append INT metadata to packets at line rate, a hardware dependency that limits the fabrics able to deploy it.

### Adaptive routing {#sec-network-fabrics-adaptive-routing}

Static routing protocols like ECMP[^fn-ecmp-flow-hashing]\index{ECMP!static flow hashing} distribute traffic by hashing flow headers to fixed paths. This approach works well for many small flows but can create persistent collisions among the small number of elephant flows\index{Elephant flow!ECMP collisions} typical of ML training. In a scenario with 4 equal-cost paths and 8 large gradient flows, an even distribution would place 2 flows on each link, whereas static hashing can place 4 flows on one link while another sits idle. In a synchronized training step, that overloaded link then determines completion time and can halve useful bandwidth.

[^fn-ecmp-flow-hashing]: **ECMP (equal-cost multi-path)**\index{ECMP!hash collision}: ECMP selects a path by hashing on the 5-tuple (source/destination IP, source/destination port, protocol), which means the same flow always takes the same path. This determinism is a feature for packet ordering but a liability for ML. Because a single AllReduce ring produces a small number of persistent flows, hash collisions are not transient statistical events but hot spots that last as long as those flows do.

Adaptive routing\index{Adaptive routing!queue-depth selection} mitigates this problem by allowing switches to select among eligible output paths using congestion information rather than only a static hash. The implementation is protocol- and device-dependent. Packet-level spraying[^fn-packet-spraying-routing]\index{Packet spraying!InfiniBand adaptive routing} can send packets of one connection over different paths, so the receiver may observe reordering. Compatible endpoint support must accept out-of-order placement or restore the transport's required ordering; the presence of InfiniBand alone does not guarantee arbitrary spraying across every path.

[^fn-packet-spraying-routing]: **Packet spraying**\index{Packet spraying!load balancing}: Unlike standard Ethernet (which hashes flows to single paths to avoid reordering), packet spraying sends individual packets of a single flow across multiple paths. This can improve use of the available $\BisectionBandwidth$ by AllReduce elephant flows when the transport can tolerate or repair reordering. The Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) specification design explicitly includes multi-path packet spraying and flexible ordering to reduce the ECMP collision problem for AI/HPC traffic [@ultraEthernet2025specification].

Ethernet fabrics can also employ **flowlet switching**\index{Flowlet switching!definition}, which changes a flow's path between bursts separated by a gap large enough to preserve packet order across the candidate paths, so its usefulness depends on how often the workload leaves such gaps relative to path delay differences. MoE expert exchanges illustrate why path diversity matters: a dense exchange among 64 expert-parallel ranks contains at most $64(64-1)=4{,}032$ directed remote rank pairs after excluding self-transfers, with active traffic governed by expert placement and token-routing sparsity. Where static-hash collisions concentrate that traffic onto a few links, adaptive routing spreads it across the provisioned $\BisectionBandwidth$. Archetype B (DLRM at Scale) creates similar exchanges when batches of embedding requests and results move among table shards, although batch and shard placement determine the traffic matrix rather than every individual lookup requiring a global exchange.

### The incast problem in ML {#sec-network-fabrics-incast}

Congestion control and adaptive routing manage flows that traverse the interior of the fabric. A different failure mode occurs at the edge, where the traffic pattern itself overwhelms a single port regardless of how much capacity the fabric interior provides.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-incast-figure
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INCAST FIGURE SCENARIO (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-congestion-cascade caption. IncastBurst (@dfn-network-fabrics-incast)
# │          reads the same inputs from this cell.
# │ Goal: Pin the caption's sender count, rates, and buffer to the registry.
# │ How: One DGX H100 SuperPOD scalable unit of NDR senders onto one 400G egress.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple

class IncastCascadeFigure:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_senders = Systems.Clusters.DgxH100SuperPodSU.total_accelerators  # one GPU per sender
    sender_bw = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth  # per port, per direction
    egress_port = Systems.Fabrics.Ethernet_400G.bandwidth
    buffer = 32 * MB  # scenario assumption: switch egress buffer

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    offered = n_senders * sender_bw
    oversub = (offered / egress_port).to_base_units().magnitude

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    # fig-alt (literal) says "GPU 1, 2, 3, and 256, with 252 more implied".
    check(n_senders == 256, "fig-alt text assumes 256 senders")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_senders_str = fmt_count(n_senders, commas=False)
    sender_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(sender_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    port_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(egress_port, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    port_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(egress_port, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    buffer_mb_str = fmt_memory(buffer, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    offered_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(offered, unit=TB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    oversub_mult_str = fmt_multiple(oversub, precision=0, commas=False)
    # The static SVG labels 50 GB/s per sender, 12.8 TB/s offered, and a 400 Gb/s egress.
    check(
        sender_bw_gb_per_s_str == "50 GB/s" and offered_tb_per_s_str == "12.8 TB/s" and port_gbit_per_s_str == "400 Gb/s",
        "incast SVG labels match the registry",
    )
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-incast-burst
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ INCAST BURST (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @dfn-network-fabrics-incast — the incast significance bullet, and
# │          the SuperPOD scalable-unit injection bandwidth (@sec-network-fabrics-dgx-superpod).
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the many-to-one incast burst onto one switch egress port.
# │ Show: 256 senders × 50 GB/s = 12.8 TB/s offered; 400 Gb/s port; 32 MB
# │       buffer holds 640 μs of one egress stream; net fill 12.75 TB/s after
# │       subtracting one egress port; overflow in ~2.5 μs; 256× oversubscription.
# │ How: offered = n_senders × beta; port = Ethernet_400G; buffer/egress and
# │      buffer/(offered − egress) give hold and overflow times.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_bandwidth, fmt_count, fmt_memory, fmt_multiple, fmt_time

class IncastBurst:
    """Many-to-one incast burst onto a single switch egress port."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    _su = Systems.Clusters.DgxH100SuperPodSU  # DGX H100 SuperPOD scalable unit
    su_nodes = _su.count  # 32 DGX nodes per scalable unit
    gpus_per_node = _su.node.accelerators_per_node  # 8 GPUs per DGX node
    n_senders = su_nodes * gpus_per_node  # 256 scalable-unit GPUs (one per egress)
    sender_bw = IncastCascadeFigure.sender_bw  # 50 GB/s per port (per direction)
    egress_port = IncastCascadeFigure.egress_port  # 400 Gb/s (50 GB/s) egress port
    buffer = IncastCascadeFigure.buffer  # scenario assumption (set in the figure cell): switch egress buffer
    feedback_rtt = 5 * microsecond  # scenario assumption: congestion-feedback round trip
    ref_cluster_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators  # SuperPOD prose: reference cluster

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    offered = n_senders * sender_bw
    su_per_ref_cluster = ref_cluster_gpus // n_senders
    oversub = (offered / egress_port).to_base_units().magnitude
    buffer_hold = buffer / egress_port  # time one egress stream takes to drain the buffer
    net_fill = offered - egress_port  # fill rate after the single egress port drains
    overflow = buffer / net_fill
    bandwidth_delay_product = egress_port * feedback_rtt

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(offered.to(TB / second).magnitude - 12.8) < 1e-6, "256 × 50 GB/s should be 12.8 TB/s")
    check(round(oversub) == 256, "Offered load should oversubscribe the egress port 256×")
    check(n_senders == IncastCascadeFigure.n_senders, "Incast definition and figure caption must use the same sender count")
    check(abs(buffer_hold.to(microsecond).magnitude - 640) < 1e-3, "32 MB / 50 GB/s should be 640 μs")
    check(overflow.to(microsecond).magnitude < 5, "Buffer should overflow in a few microseconds")
    check(abs(bandwidth_delay_product.to(KB).magnitude - 250) < 1e-6, "50 GB/s × 5 μs should be 250 KB")
    check(ref_cluster_gpus % n_senders == 0, "Reference cluster should be a whole number of scalable units")
    # SuperPOD prose spells these counts as words; fail loudly if the registry moves them.
    check(int(gpus_per_node) == 8, "SuperPOD prose says eight H100 GPUs per node")
    check(su_per_ref_cluster == 4, "SuperPOD prose says four scalable units")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_senders_str = fmt_count(n_senders, commas=False)
    su_nodes_str = fmt_count(su_nodes, commas=False, label="node")
    gpus_per_node_word_str = MarkdownStr("eight")  # guarded above
    su_per_ref_cluster_word_str = MarkdownStr("four")  # guarded above
    ref_cluster_gpus_str = fmt_count(ref_cluster_gpus, commas=True, label="GPU")
    n_senders_gpus_str = fmt_count(n_senders, commas=False, label="GPU")
    sender_bw_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(sender_bw, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    offered_tb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(offered, unit=TB / second, precision=1, commas=False)
    port_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(egress_port, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    buffer_mb_str = fmt_memory(buffer, unit=MB, precision=0, commas=False)
    buffer_hold_us_str = fmt_time(buffer_hold, microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    feedback_rtt_us_str = fmt_time(feedback_rtt, microsecond, precision=0, commas=False)
    bandwidth_delay_product_kb_str = fmt_memory(bandwidth_delay_product, unit=KB, precision=0, commas=False)
    oversubscription_mult_str = fmt_multiple(oversub, precision=0, commas=False)
    overflow_us_str = fmt_time(overflow, microsecond, precision=1, commas=False)
```

::: {#dfn-network-fabrics-incast .callout-definition title="Incast"}

***Incast***\index{Incast!definition} is a many-to-one ML cluster traffic pattern in which a large number of senders simultaneously transmit data to a single receiver port. It concentrates line-rate traffic from multiple sources into a single switch queue, and it can overflow the buffer if the burst outlasts the available buffering and control response, even when the rest of the fabric is uncongested.

1.  **Significance**: Flat aggregation, synchronized storage reads, or other fan-in phases can direct many senders toward one receiver. The deliberately worst-case scenario here assumes a RoCE fabric whose ports all run at `{python} IncastBurst.port_gbit_per_s_str`. In it, `{python} IncastBurst.n_senders_str` senders each transmit at `{python} IncastBurst.sender_bw_gb_per_s_str` toward one switch egress, producing `{python} IncastBurst.offered_tb_per_s_str` of offered load against a `{python} IncastBurst.port_gbit_per_s_str` port. A `{python} IncastBurst.buffer_mb_str` buffer then overflows in about `{python} IncastBurst.overflow_us_str` under the stated assumptions, after which the switch either drops packets or, in a PFC deployment, pauses its upstream neighbors. The example is a stress bound, not the traffic matrix of a ring AllReduce.
2.  **Distinction**: Unlike general congestion (which occurs on shared internal links when aggregate traffic exceeds link capacity), incast is an endpoint bottleneck. It occurs even if every internal spine and leaf link is completely uncongested, because the bottleneck is the single destination port, not the fabric interior.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Incast is not necessarily rare or unpredictable. Training jobs create it on a schedule, whenever many GPUs read dataset shards from or write checkpoints to the same storage node, and in the aggregation step of a tree or hierarchical reduction, where several ranks send partial sums to one parent. A gradient ring is different; its point-to-point flows can still collide at a shared egress, but that is a hot spot rather than many-to-one incast. The severity depends on the collective algorithm, topology, routing, and oversubscription, so it must be measured and mitigated rather than treated as an edge case.

:::

In a worst-case incast, `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.offered_tb_per_s_str` of offered traffic from `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.n_senders_str` senders converges on a single `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gbit_per_s_str` (`{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gb_per_s_str`) egress (@fig-congestion-cascade). Each sender injects at `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.sender_bw_gb_per_s_str`. The buffer fills over a finite interval; control feedback can reduce arrivals, drops can discard excess traffic, or backpressure can move the queueing upstream. Whether that pressure spreads depends on shared queues and the paths carrying the traffic. Let the aggregate arrival rate to one egress be $\EgressArrivalRate$, the egress service rate be $\EgressServiceRate$, and the instantaneous queue occupancy be $\EgressQueueOccupancy(\TimeInstant)$. While a burst persists and $\EgressArrivalRate > \EgressServiceRate$, the queue grows at the net rate

$$
\EgressQueueOccupancy(\TimeInstant) = \min\!\left(\EgressBufferCapacity,\; \EgressQueueOccupancy(0) + (\EgressArrivalRate-\EgressServiceRate)\TimeInstant\right),
$$

where $\EgressBufferCapacity$ is the finite buffer capacity. The ratio $\EgressPortUtilization=\EgressArrivalRate/\EgressServiceRate$ distinguishes a drainable workload from sustained overload: for $\EgressPortUtilization<1$, idle intervals can drain the queue; as long-run $\EgressPortUtilization$ approaches one, less slack remains to absorb bursts; and for $\EgressPortUtilization>1$, occupancy must reach a control threshold or the buffer limit if the overload persists. This is a packet queue, distinct from the request queues of an inference server. Serialization and propagation set the unloaded path latency, whereas queued bytes add approximately $\EgressQueueOccupancy/\EgressServiceRate$ of waiting time.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
⇄ **Contrast:** Request queues, whose arrival and service rates set serving latency rather than switch buffer occupancy, are developed in @sec-appdx-inference-scale-queuing-theory-batched-inference-bbf0.
:::

In the deliberately worst-case incast above, $\EgressPortUtilization$ is `{python} IncastBurst.oversubscription_mult_str`, so the `{python} IncastBurst.buffer_mb_str` buffer fills in about `{python} IncastBurst.overflow_us_str`. Once full, that buffer represents `{python} IncastBurst.buffer_hold_us_str` of egress waiting time. By contrast, the bandwidth-delay product\index{Bandwidth-delay product!buffer distinction} for the `{python} IncastBurst.port_gbit_per_s_str` egress and an illustrative `{python} IncastBurst.feedback_rtt_us_str` feedback round trip is only `{python} IncastBurst.bandwidth_delay_product_kb_str`; it measures data in flight on the path, not the buffering needed to absorb an arbitrary fan-in burst. ECN\index{ECN!reaction window} must mark early enough for feedback to arrive before exhaustion; PFC can prevent a drop, but its backpressure can spread congestion. A larger buffer extends the reaction window at the cost of a larger tail-latency bound.

::: {#fig-congestion-cascade fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**A True Incast Burst**: This deliberately worst-case fan-in scenario sends `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.n_senders_str` sources at `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.sender_bw_gb_per_s_str` toward one `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gbit_per_s_str` (`{python} IncastCascadeFigure.port_gb_per_s_str`) egress with a `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.buffer_mb_str` buffer. The `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.offered_tb_per_s_str` offered load oversubscribes the destination egress by `{python} IncastCascadeFigure.oversub_mult_str`. Flat aggregation or synchronized reads can create this pattern; bandwidth-optimal ring AllReduce does not, because each rank exchanges point-to-point chunks." fig-alt="Four labeled sender GPUs, GPU 1, 2, 3, and 256, with a dashed placeholder box labeled 252 more emitting a fan of fainter lines, each send at 50 GB/s along lines that converge into one thick arrow entering a switch egress port. The port's 32 MB buffer is drawn as a row of full red cells marked drops or PAUSE upstream, and a dashed red PAUSE arrow runs from the switch back to the top of the sender column. A thin 400 Gb/s arrow leaves the port to one receiver. Below, two bars drawn to the same scale compare rates: a long bar labeled offered, 12.8 TB/s, and a sliver labeled egress, 50 GB/s, with the note 256 times oversubscribed."}
![](images/svg/incast-flow.svg)

:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Incast paragraph below — cluster GPU count
class NetworkIncastClusterRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators, commas=True, label="GPU")
```

Synchronized ML traffic is susceptible to both true fan-in and shared-egress hot spots. When a layer finishes backward computation, many ranks can inject traffic at once, and flat or hierarchical aggregation phases can create true fan-in. Production clusters mitigate both cases along three complementary dimensions:

1. **Time.** Layer-staggering\index{Incast!layer-staggering mitigation} triggers each gradient bucket's AllReduce as soon as backpropagation produces it. Final-layer gradients reduce while earlier layers are still computing, so communication is spread across the backward pass instead of released as one synchronized burst. The same staggering is communication-computation overlap\index{Communication-computation overlap!incast mitigation}, so it also hides transfer time behind the backward computation that remains.
2. **Space.** Collective algorithm selection\index{Incast!algorithm selection mitigation} bounds fan-in at individual switch ports. Hierarchical and rail-local reductions aggregate gradients in stages so that no single port must absorb all senders at once, and topology-aware placement keeps concurrent ring flows off oversubscribed ports.
3. **Priority.** Quality of service (QoS) classification\index{Quality of service!priority traffic} tags gradient traffic with the highest service class to reduce interference from background storage or management traffic; shared links, buffers, and arbitration still constrain isolation.

These mitigations spread the burst in time, space, and priority, but they do not eliminate congestion or tail latency. The question becomes how to build end-to-end clusters that perform despite these realities.

## Level 5 Cluster Design and Case Studies {#sec-network-fabrics-cluster}

The final level of the stack is cluster design\index{Cluster design!gradient bus integration}, where wires, transport, topology, and congestion control combine into a coherent system. The goal of cluster design is to provide an end-to-end gradient bus that makes thousands of distributed GPUs feel like a single machine. At this level, the abstraction layers collapse into concrete engineering decisions: which cables to buy, how to wire the racks, which protocol to deploy, and how to validate that the resulting fabric delivers the bandwidth the training job expects. Two representative large-scale architectures, one built on InfiniBand and one on Ethernet, illuminate the trade-offs that define ML infrastructure [@nvidia2023dgxSuperpodH100; @meta2024genaiInfrastructure; @gangidi2024rdma].

### The GPU-to-GPU "gradient bus" {#sec-network-fabrics-gradient-bus}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: calc-vol2-network-fabrics-cluster-recap
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Gradient bus — NVLink/IB cliff and SuperPOD specs.
class NetworkFabricsClusterRecap:
    ib_ndr = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth
    nvlink = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth  # 900 GB/s bidirectional aggregate (for display)
    nvlink_perdir = Hardware.Cloud.H100.nvlink.bandwidth_per_direction  # 450 GB/s one-way for the cliff ratio
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    # Per-direction-vs-per-port cliff (honest 9x; 900-vs-50 would double-count to 18x)
    nvlink_to_ib_ratio_mult_str = fmt_multiple(round((nvlink_perdir / ib_ndr).to_base_units().magnitude), precision=0, commas=False)
    nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(nvlink, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

In a well-designed cluster, the network fabric acts as a scheduler-aware extension of the system bus, not a passive pipe. The ~`{python} NetworkFabricsClusterRecap.nvlink_to_ib_ratio_mult_str` per-direction cliff between NVLink and one external port, measured at the start of this chapter, is the gap the cluster must hide. Communication-computation overlap\index{Communication-computation overlap!latency hiding}, which the Fleet Law credits as $\OverlappedTime$, is the first mechanism for hiding it, through the same layer-staggered AllReduce launch that spreads incast bursts in @sec-network-fabrics-incast. Overlap cannot hide the last mile of the exchange, because the gradients computed at the end of backpropagation have little computation left behind which to hide their transfer (@sec-communication-overlap).

Placement is the second mechanism, because it decides which communication crosses each boundary. The placement that the bandwidth hierarchy of @sec-compute-bandwidth-hierarchy sets, tensor parallelism inside the NVLink domain with pipeline stages and data-parallel replicas spanning nodes, becomes a wiring rule at cluster scale, because each fabric tier must be provisioned for the traffic placed on it. The links between nodes must meet the pipeline's\index{Pipeline parallelism!network hierarchy} activation-transfer budget, which physical adjacency alone does not guarantee. The full fabric carries the data-parallel\index{Data parallelism!network hierarchy} exchanges, which gradient accumulation makes less frequent and overlap partly hides. Production designs therefore differ mainly in how they provision that outermost tier, as the two that follow show.

### NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD architecture {#sec-network-fabrics-dgx-superpod}

The NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD, a concrete implementation of the gradient bus, provisions the outermost tier by obtaining losslessness from the link layer and aligning the wiring with the data-parallel ranks, so that the fabric's tail behavior depends on hardware mechanisms rather than on congestion tuning. It connects DGX H100 nodes using an NDR InfiniBand network [@nvidia2023dgxSuperpodH100]. Each node acts as a dense compute island, with `{python} IncastBurst.gpus_per_node_word_str` H100 GPUs connected via NVSwitch to provide `{python} NetworkFabricsClusterRecap.nvlink_h100_gb_per_s_str` of internal bandwidth. Externally, each GPU pairs with a ConnectX-7 NIC delivering `{python} NetworkFabricsClusterRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` of injection bandwidth. Across a standard scalable unit of `{python} IncastBurst.su_nodes_str` (`{python} IncastBurst.n_senders_gpus_str`), this yields an aggregate injection bandwidth of `{python} IncastBurst.offered_tb_per_s_str` (`{python} IncastBurst.n_senders_str` $\times$ `{python} IncastBurst.sender_bw_gb_per_s_str`), the rate the scalable unit can offer the fabric when every GPU transmits at once.

This architecture connects all five levels of the network model into a single chain. At the wire (Level 1), it standardizes on `{python} NetworkFabricsClusterRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` NDR links, choosing copper or optics by the reach between each node and its leaf and between leaf and spine. Because those links run InfiniBand's native credit-based flow control at the transport layer (Level 2), they provide a lossless medium without the pause-cascade fragility of Ethernet PFC. Above the transport, the topology (Level 3) arranges the switches as a rail-optimized fat-tree\index{Rail-optimized topology!DGX SuperPOD implementation}, aligning GPU rails across each scalable unit so that same-rail traffic stays close while cross-rail traffic traverses the spine layer (replacing the simpler per-rack ToR allocation used earlier to illustrate switch radix). When cross-rank traffic climbs to the spine, hardware-based adaptive routing (Level 4) selects among spine paths to preserve bisection behavior. Finally, at the cluster level (Level 5), additional switching joins multiple SuperPOD scalable units into larger fleets [@nvidia2023dgxSuperpodH100]: for the 175B-parameter model, `{python} IncastBurst.su_per_ref_cluster_word_str` SuperPOD scalable units wire together so that `{python} IncastBurst.ref_cluster_gpus_str` function as a single synchronous instrument.

### Meta Grand Teton platform {#sec-network-fabrics-grand-teton}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-grand-teton
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ META GRAND TETON CLUSTERS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-grand-teton opening paragraph.
# │ Goal: Pin the disclosed cluster size and endpoint rate to the registry.
# │ How: Systems.Clusters.Meta_GenAI_H100_24K_RoCE / _IB (3,072 Grand Teton
# │      nodes × 8 H100) on Systems.Fabrics.RoCE_400G / InfiniBand_NDR.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth

class GrandTetonClusters:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    roce = Systems.Clusters.Meta_GenAI_H100_24K_RoCE
    ib = Systems.Clusters.Meta_GenAI_H100_24K_IB

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(roce.total_accelerators == ib.total_accelerators, "Both Meta clusters have the same GPU count")
    check(roce.fabric.bandwidth == ib.fabric.bandwidth, "Both Meta clusters use the same endpoint rate")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_value_str = fmt(roce.total_accelerators, precision=0, commas=True)
    endpoint_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(roce.fabric.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Meta's Grand Teton clusters take the opposite approach, accepting Ethernet's congestion-tuning burden in exchange for multi-vendor supply and shared operations. Meta disclosed two Grand Teton-based `{python} GrandTetonClusters.n_gpus_value_str`-H100 clusters: one using RoCE over an Arista/OCP Ethernet fabric and one using NVIDIA Quantum-2 InfiniBand, both with `{python} GrandTetonClusters.endpoint_gbit_per_s_str` endpoints. Meta used both for Llama 3 training and reported ongoing Llama 3 training on the RoCE cluster [@meta2024genaiInfrastructure]. Ethernet lets Meta source switches from multiple vendors and reuse the optical infrastructure and management tooling of its front-end serving fleet, avoiding the operational silo of a dedicated InfiniBand island.

Meta's RoCE study shows how Level 4 choices affect the complete fabric. It describes PFC watchdogs for long-duration pause events, iterative routing designs beyond plain ECMP, future-oriented flowlet switching experiments, and a 400G deployment in which DCQCN tuning proved difficult enough that Meta proceeded without DCQCN while relying on PFC plus higher-layer collective controls [@gangidi2024rdma]. The lesson is to validate the combination of endpoint behavior, routing, and flow control under the intended collective traffic. Large-transfer throughput alone does not establish small-message latency or recovery tails, and those results cannot be inferred from the Ethernet or InfiniBand label. Small-message latency matters in training through frequent small exchanges, which expose startup cost even when a full step lasts seconds, and in serving to a degree set by model partitioning, request shape, and service-level objectives (SLOs).

These case studies close the five-level stack by showing how the physical wire, transport protocol, topology, and congestion controls become one production fabric. The remaining operational problem is not how to build a single fast cluster, but how to share that expensive substrate across teams and workloads without sacrificing the predictable performance that training demands.

## Network Virtualization {#sec-network-fabrics-virtualization}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-virtualization-idle-cost
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ MULTI-TENANCY SHARING SCENARIO (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-virtualization opening paragraph, SR-IOV
# │          rate split, and the checkpoint-burst contention scenario.
# │ Goal: Size the bandwidth policy, VF rate, and neighbor checkpoint burst.
# │ How: VF rate = NIC line rate / VF count; burst time = write size / line rate.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt_percent

class VirtualizationIdleCost:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    training_share = 0.80  # scenario assumption: bisection share reserved for the training job
    n_vfs = 8  # scenario assumption: SR-IOV virtual functions carved from one NIC
    nic_bw = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth
    ckpt_write = 100 * GB  # scenario assumption: neighboring job's checkpoint burst

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    vf_rate = nic_bw / n_vfs
    ckpt_time = ckpt_write / nic_bw

    # ┌── 3. GUARD ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    check(n_vfs == 8, "Prose spells the VF count as 'eight'")
    check(abs(ckpt_time.to(second).magnitude - 2) < 1e-9, "100 GB at 50 GB/s should take 2 s")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
    training_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(training_share, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    other_share_pct_str = fmt_percent(1 - training_share, precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")
    n_vfs_word_str = MarkdownStr("eight")  # guarded above
    vf_rate_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(vf_rate, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    ckpt_gb_str = fmt_memory(ckpt_write, unit=GB, precision=0, commas=False)
    ckpt_s_str = fmt_time(ckpt_time, second, precision=0, commas=False)
```

When a single training job leaves racks or spine links idle between runs, operators carve the cluster among multiple tenants and jobs, only to discover that a neighbor's checkpoint burst or evaluation sweep can starve a synchronous AllReduce across shared NICs and switch buffers. Network virtualization\index{Network virtualization!multi-tenancy} must make sharing compatible with bandwidth allocations, latency targets, and access isolation. These requirements interact because tenants still share physical links and buffers. A proposed policy might reserve `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.training_share_pct_str` of the cluster's $\BisectionBandwidth$ for training and allocate the remaining `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.other_share_pct_str` to inference and preprocessing. Enforcing that policy requires admission control and compatible scheduling along the relevant paths; a virtual NIC or separate traffic class alone does not guarantee the end-to-end share.

### Hardware NIC virtualization with SR-IOV {#sec-network-fabrics-sriov}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: SR-IOV and QoS — NDR line rate.
class IbNdrVirtualizationRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Routing multi-tenant traffic through a hypervisor's software virtual switch reintroduces the exact host-CPU overhead and microsecond jitter that RDMA was built to bypass. Cloud providers instead expose NIC resources to virtualized GPU instances through **single-root I/O virtualization (SR-IOV)**\index{SR-IOV!definition}, a standard that allows a physical NIC to present multiple **virtual functions (VFs)**\index{Virtual function!definition}. Each VF exposes its own hardware queues, doorbell registers, and DMA mappings, which software can assign to a workload. A directly assigned VF can remove host software mediation from the active DMA path, while drivers and virtualization software still configure access and manage the device. Performance depends on the NIC, I/O placement, and competing traffic. Because VFs share physical resources, placement logic must reserve NIC capacity and QoS policy alongside GPUs rather than treat the network as an unbounded pool.

However, hardware-level isolation still needs explicit bandwidth policy. SR-IOV exposes multiple VFs that share the NIC's physical resources; administrators can add per-VF or per-group QoS policies to cap or guarantee bandwidth, such as assigning `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.n_vfs_word_str` VFs `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.vf_rate_gbit_per_s_str` each on a `{python} IbNdrVirtualizationRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` NIC. For the 175B-parameter model training on a multi-tenant cluster, that configured partitioning can prevent a neighboring tenant from stealing bandwidth, but it also enforces a hard ceiling on peak throughput. The training job must be architected to operate within this slice, as no amount of software optimization can burst beyond the configured VF limit.

### Traffic isolation and quality of service {#sec-network-fabrics-qos}

Per-VF rate caps bound what each tenant injects at the NIC, but traffic from different tenants still merges on the fabric's shared switch buffers and spine links. When the 175B model is midway through a gradient AllReduce and a neighboring job initiates a `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.ckpt_gb_str` checkpoint save, that burst occupies a `{python} IbNdrVirtualizationRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str` port for `{python} VirtualizationIdleCost.ckpt_s_str` at full line rate. It can also claim a large share of the shared spine links for that interval, which stretches every AllReduce whose traffic crosses them. To prevent this noisy-neighbor effect inside the fabric, high-performance switches rely on **quality of service (QoS)**\index{Quality of service!definition} mechanisms that enforce fairness at the packet and queue level.

InfiniBand isolates traffic through virtual lanes (VLs)\index{Virtual lane!traffic isolation}, which maintain separate credit and buffer state within a physical link across up to 16 lanes (one of them reserved for subnet management) [@infiniband2000spec]. If a storage burst exhausts the credits of its own lane, a gradient lane with available credits can continue transmitting, even though both lanes still share link bandwidth and arbitration. Ethernet and RoCE fabrics achieve a similar separation through device-dependent **traffic class**\index{Traffic class!definition} mappings and queue policies, where **enhanced transmission selection**\index{Enhanced transmission selection!definition} allocates service among traffic classes and switches may also partition buffer and forwarding resources into **network slices**\index{Network slice!definition}. Across both stacks, these mechanisms reduce interference only when classification, resource allocation, and scheduling agree along the entire path, because shared priorities or buffer pools can still couple tenants.

Virtualization solves the sharing problem but makes performance diagnosis harder. When a training job slows down on a multi-tenant cluster, the cause could be a physical link degradation, a noisy neighbor exceeding its bandwidth allocation, or a misconfigured QoS policy. Systematic monitoring is essential to distinguish these cases.

## Monitoring and Debugging {#sec-network-fabrics-monitoring}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-silent-waste
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SILENT WASTE BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-monitoring — the silent-waste paragraph.
# │
# │ Goal: Quantify the GPU-hours and dollars a slow transceiver wastes over a
# │       30-day run before any alarm fires.
# │ Show: 10 percent BW loss → 2-3 percent per-iteration slowdown →
# │       ~15,000-22,000 wasted GPU-hours → ~\$30,000-\$44,000 at \$2/GPU-hour.
# │ How: total GPU-hours = N × days × 24; waste = total × slowdown; cost =
# │      waste × Fleet.GpuHourRef (in-service accelerator-hour). Range rounded to thousands.
# │
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_count, fmt_percent, fmt_percent_range, fmt_range, fmt_usd

class SilentWaste:
    """Silent waste a degraded transceiver inflicts on a 30-day run."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus = Systems.Clusters.Training_1K.total_accelerators
    gpu_hour_rate = Infrastructure.Pricing.Fleet.GpuHourRef.rate  # fleet price canon, per in-service accelerator-hour
    bw_loss = 0.10  # scenario assumption: bandwidth loss from a degraded transceiver
    slowdown_lo = 0.02  # scenario assumption: per-iteration slowdown (low end)
    slowdown_hi = 0.03  # scenario assumption: per-iteration slowdown (high end)
    run_days = 30  # scenario assumption: training-run duration
    n_links = SerDesPowerBudget.n_links  # same fabric link count as the SerDes power estimate
    p_link_degraded = 0.001  # scenario assumption: point-in-time probability that one link is degraded

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    total_gpu_hours = n_gpus * run_days * 24
    waste_lo = round(total_gpu_hours * slowdown_lo / 1000) * 1000
    waste_hi = round(total_gpu_hours * slowdown_hi / 1000) * 1000
    _rate = gpu_hour_rate.to(USD / hour).magnitude
    cost_lo = round(waste_lo * _rate / 1000) * 1000
    cost_hi = round(waste_hi * _rate / 1000) * 1000
    expected_degraded = n_links * p_link_degraded
    p_any_degraded = 1 - (1 - p_link_degraded) ** n_links

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(total_gpu_hours == 737280, "1,024 GPUs × 30 days × 24 h should be 737,280 GPU-hours")
    check(waste_lo < waste_hi, "Low waste estimate must be below the high estimate")
    check(cost_hi < 100_000, "Silent waste should be tens of thousands of dollars, not millions")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    n_gpus_str = fmt_count(n_gpus, commas=True, label="GPU")
    bw_loss_pct_str = fmt_percent(bw_loss, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    slowdown_pct_range_str = fmt_percent_range(slowdown_lo, slowdown_hi, precision=0, commas=False, style='prose')
    run_days_str = fmt(run_days, precision=0, commas=False)
    waste_gpu_hours_range_str = fmt_range(waste_lo, waste_hi, precision=0, kind="number")
    waste_cost_range_str = fmt_range(cost_lo, cost_hi, precision=0, kind="usd")
    gpu_hour_rate_str = fmt_usd(_rate, precision=0, commas=False, per="GPU-hour")
    n_links_str = fmt(n_links, precision=0, commas=True)
    p_link_pct_str = fmt_percent(p_link_degraded, precision=1, commas=False, style="prose")
    expected_degraded_str = fmt(expected_degraded, precision=0, commas=False)
    p_any_pct_str = fmt_percent(round(p_any_degraded, 2), precision=0, commas=False, style="prose")  # rounded to whole percent
```

Network performance problems in ML clusters are insidious because they show up as **silent waste**\index{Silent waste!definition} rather than explicit failures. A degraded transceiver causing a `{python} SilentWaste.bw_loss_pct_str` reduction in effective bandwidth might slow each training iteration by only `{python} SilentWaste.slowdown_pct_range_str`. The slowdown is small because the lost bandwidth stretches only the exposed communication share of the step (the `{python} NonBlockingOversubscription.comm_pct_str` assumed in the oversubscription estimate, less whatever overlap hides), and stretches it by roughly the inverse of the bandwidth that remains. A drift that small is easily masked by the natural variance of checkpointing or data loading. Over a `{python} SilentWaste.run_days_str`-day training run on `{python} SilentWaste.n_gpus_str`, this invisible drag accumulates to roughly `{python} SilentWaste.waste_gpu_hours_range_str` wasted GPU-hours, burning about `{python} SilentWaste.waste_cost_range_str` at `{python} SilentWaste.gpu_hour_rate_str` without triggering a single alarm. Traditional IT monitoring tools like SNMP or ICMP ping measure connectivity, not the sustained throughput required by RDMA. Effective observability\index{Monitoring!network} requires a three-layer approach: **physical monitoring**\index{Physical monitoring!definition} (FEC errors, signal attenuation), **transport monitoring**\index{Transport monitoring!definition} (PFC pause frames, retransmission rates), and **application monitoring**\index{Application monitoring!definition} (NCCL algorithmic bandwidth) [@jeaugey2017nccl; @gangidi2024rdma]. The three layers retrace the five-level model from the top down. Application monitoring observes the collective that Level 5 integrates, transport monitoring observes the Level 2 recovery and Level 4 congestion machinery, and physical monitoring observes the Level 1 wire. Only by correlating signals across these layers can operators detect that a "slow training run" is caused by a single degraded cable in one rack.

### Link-level telemetry {#sec-network-fabrics-link-telemetry}

Hardware counters test whether the deployed path still behaves as assumed. Switch and NIC port counters\index{Port counters!fabric telemetry} report transmitted and received data, transmit discards, symbol errors, and link-down events; on InfiniBand a utility such as `perfquery` reads them, and Ethernet/RoCE devices expose the equivalent telemetry through their own management interfaces [@linuxManpages2026perfquery]. Data counters measure utilization, discards warrant investigation against the port's traffic and recovery policy, and symbol errors and link-down events are evidence of a degrading signal. Correlating those counters with link rate, lane state, and transport behavior narrows the cause; a counter alone does not identify a defective cable or transceiver.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: network-fabrics-hdr-ndr-reference
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ HDR/NDR BANDWIDTH REFERENCE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-network-fabrics-link-telemetry—silent degradation from
# │          HDR fallback; @sec-network-fabrics-fallacies—bandwidth fallacy.
# │
# │ Goal: Provide HDR bandwidth for comparison against NDR in monitoring and
# │       fallacy discussions.
# │ Show: ~200 Gb/s HDR vs ~400 Gb/s NDR.
# │ How: Preserve the Pint bandwidth quantity through the guard and formatter.
# │
# │ Used by: silent degradation paragraph below; Fallacies section.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

class IbHdrReference:
    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    hdr_bw = Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_HDR.bandwidth

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (The Compute) ────────────────────────────────────────
    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    from mlsysim.fmt import check, fmt, fmt_bandwidth

    check(round(hdr_bw.to(Gbps).magnitude) == 200, "HDR bandwidth should be 200 Gb/s")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_hdr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(hdr_bw, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_bandwidth

# ┌── LEGO ───────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: Monitoring — NDR negotiated speed checks.
class IbNdrMonitoringRecap:
    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=Gbps, precision=0, commas=False)
    ib_ndr_gb_per_s_str = fmt_bandwidth(Systems.Fabrics.InfiniBand_NDR.bandwidth, unit=GB / second, precision=0, commas=False)
```

Polling link state alongside traffic counters can reveal **silent degradation**\index{Silent degradation!definition}. A link operating at HDR (`{python} IbHdrReference.ib_hdr_gbit_per_s_str`) rather than the expected NDR rate (`{python} IbNdrMonitoringRecap.ib_ndr_gbit_per_s_str`) can remain connected while offering half the expected bandwidth. A link that trains with two of its four lanes active after a connector fault fails the same way: it stays up while its bandwidth is halved. Both cases are visible only when negotiated rate and lane state are compared with the deployment baseline. For `{python} SilentWaste.n_gpus_str` and roughly `{python} SilentWaste.n_links_str` links, the assumed `{python} SilentWaste.p_link_pct_str` point-in-time degradation probability gives `{python} SilentWaste.expected_degraded_str` degraded links in expectation and, under independent events, a `{python} SilentWaste.p_any_pct_str` probability of at least one degradation. This probability measures something different from the daily figure in notebook \ref{nbk-network-fabrics-probability-transceiver-degradation}. That notebook asks how often a new degradation begins; this one asks how many degraded links are present at any moment. Standing prevalence is roughly the onset rate times how long a degraded link stays in service, and silent degradation, by definition, stays in service until someone looks, so prevalence can far exceed what a small daily onset rate suggests. Both rates are scenario assumptions rather than measured fleet data. A job slows when an affected path limits its required traffic; fleet-wide exposure alone does not determine the job's slowdown. When the degraded link lies on a ring AllReduce's path, however, the cost reaches every participant, because each round waits for its slowest hop and the whole ring proceeds at the pace of that one link.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
